AC: if the anchor would truncate, it is surfaced (warning) rather than silently narrowing
AC: regression test with two session-state files where the newer one belongs to a DIFFERENT session/epic than the one closing
2026-07-28 (proyecto_anita close, t-2251): NOT A TRADE — OVER-reach still happens AFTER the t-2491 fix. LAST_CLOSE resolved to 2026-07-28T15:25:20Z and COMMIT_COUNT came back 8, of which 2 (676d4dd9, 9b6bda3c) belonged to a concurrent t-2285 session that merged to main AFTER that anchor timestamp. So the max-across-files anchor over-reaches when a concurrent session commits after your anchor, and under-reaches when a concurrent session CLOSES before you (the 2026-07-27 case above). Direction depends purely on whether the other session's close lands before or after your window opens — it is not a stable trade of one failure for the other, and a fix that only addresses under-reach will leave the over-reach half live. IMPLICATION FOR THE FIX: no session-state timestamp can be correct here, because the anchor is a wall-clock proxy for 'my work' in a repo where 'my work' is not contiguous in time. Derive the range from the closing session's OWN commits (first commit this session ^..HEAD), the same shape t-2242 applied to Step 1b. SECOND REPRODUCTION, 2026-07-28 — worse than the first, and it points at the fix.

First repro truncated the window (3 commits counted for a 10-commit session). This one EXCLUDED IT ENTIRELY: COMMIT_COUNT came back 0.

Timeline, all UTC:
  15:22:17  this session's own previous close  (epic "close")
  15:57:00  this session commits 24e6ee08 (t-2503 rule change)
  15:57:16  this session commits d7de06ed (merge)
  15:58:57  CONCURRENT session writes its close state (orphan/default)
The global max is 15:58:57 — 1m41s AFTER this session's last commit — so `--since` that timestamp matched nothing and the gate computed a zero-commit window. A zero-commit window is not merely wrong: gate-and-evidence.md Step 1 treats "no commits, no changes" as a READ-ONLY session and short-circuits to a one-line handoff, skipping the snapshot entirely. So the failure escalates from "queues too little" to "queues nothing and declares the session read-only".

The severity ordering is now clear: over-reach double-extracts (visible, recoverable), truncation loses part (invisible), zero-window loses everything AND misclassifies the session.

WHAT WORKED. Anchoring on the newest written_at for THIS session's own epic — `jq '.[] | select(.epic=="close") | .state.written_at'` — returned 15:22:17 and yielded the correct 11-commit window. That is candidate fix #1 already listed above, now empirically confirmed on a live case. Recommend implementing it as: prefer the newest state whose epic matches the epic this close will write to; fall back to the global max only when no such entry exists (first close for that epic); never let an entry from a different epic/session move the anchor forward.

Note the interaction with the Step 1 read-only short-circuit — whatever fix lands must also ensure a zero-commit window caused by anchoring cannot be mistaken for a genuinely read-only session.

STRUCTURAL LIMIT (new — not previously recorded here). A contiguous range A..B cannot express a non-contiguous commit set. Sessions interleave on dev, so even a CORRECT start-anchor yields a range containing another session's commits. This is why the 2026-07-28 epic-scoped attempt produced an 11-commit window holding only 2 own commits: the anchor was right and the range was still ~80% contamination. Killing over-reach therefore needs per-commit recording PLUS a --commits LIST interface into close-snapshot.sh (which today accepts only --git-range). Anchor fixes and over-reach fixes are separate problems; no anchor change of any kind can solve the second.

STORE AUDIT (live, thebrana, 2026-07-28). All 24 session-state files return has_session_id: false — the store carries NO session identity at all; it is keyed by epic alone. Key collision is already live: three files claim epic "harness-core" (session-state-harness-core.json, session-state-async-close.json, session-state-thinking.json), i.e. the filename slug and the inner epic field have drifted apart. CORRECTION TO A NATURAL ASSUMPTION. Overwriting is NOT destroying past work: `brana session history` is append-only and retains prior states (verified — the concurrent 15:58:57 Telegram session sits between this lane's 15:22:17 and 16:01:47 closes). What is lost is IDENTITY, not data. History is a flat chronological list with nothing distinguishing whose lane an entry belongs to, which is why a fresh session cannot tell whether a handoff is its own or a parallel lane's.

ROOT CAUSE, RESTATED (supersedes "newest close anywhere is the wrong question"). ADR-065 defines epic as "what we're building, empty = feature done" — a DELIVERABLE. A lane is an EXECUTION CONTEXT. Keying session handoffs by epic uses a "what" as a "where", so two parallel sessions building toward one deliverable are the same key by construction. Not a keying bug; a category error in the choice of key.

THE PRIMITIVE ALREADY EXISTS IN THE BACKLOG. task -> task.branch -> worktree -> session is already 1:1, enforced by git-discipline's worktree HARD RULE; `backlog start` already writes task.branch and already claims the lane by branch (claims_claim claimant "agent:{branch}:session"). Constraint: the key must be captured at session START, not read at close — 15 of 24 files record branch "dev" because closes happen after merge, so branch collapses at close time.

`git worktree remove` deletes `.git/worktrees/<name>/` in full, `logs/HEAD` included. Measured

WHAT THIS HITS HERE, specifically:

tasks.context:
All three hit live 2026-07-27 in a single thebrana session.

1. EXIT CODE THROUGH A PIPE. `bash validate.sh 2>&1 | tail -25; echo "EXIT=$?"` printed EXIT=0 — that is tail's status, not validate.sh's. The real result was unknown and had to be re-run. This is a direct extension of what parallel-bash.md ALREADY teaches: it recommends `cmd; echo EXIT:$?`, which is correct, but context-budget.md simultaneously pushes piping into filters to keep output small. Compose the two recommendations and the exit code silently becomes the filter's. That is why this belongs IN parallel-bash.md rather than a new rule file — the rule's own idiom is one pipe away from lying.

2. SELF-MATCHING pgrep. `until ! pgrep -f "bash validate.sh"; do sleep 10; done` never terminates: pgrep -f matches full command lines, including the watcher loop's own, which contains the literal pattern. Four such loops spun until the user noticed them. Fix: bracket one character — `pgrep -f "[b]ash validate.sh"` — or match on a pidfile instead.

3. REDUNDANT BACKGROUND POLLING. Those wait loops were unnecessary in the first place: Bash run_in_background already fires a completion notification. Polling on top of it is waste, and a buggy poller can outlive the work it watches. The harness had already blocked a chained `sleep` for this reason; the until-loop was the same mistake in another shape.

Corollary worth including: verify a DEPLOY by reading the deployed artifact, not the installer's exit code. bootstrap.sh was killed at a 2-minute timeout (exit 143) mid-deploy; the re-run exited 0, but only grepping the deployed files confirmed the fixes actually landed.

Keep it short — parallel-bash.md is currently ~900B and the rules dir favours brevity. Do not create a 29th rule file unless review says the combined doc is too long.

AC: parallel-bash.md covers the pipe/exit-code trap with a WRONG/RIGHT example using PIPESTATUS or a redirect
AC: covers the pgrep self-match with the bracket fix
AC: states that run_in_background notifies on completion, so wait-loops are usually redundant
AC: validate.sh green (it lint-checks rule frontmatter)

Found live 2026-07-28 on the second /brana:close --continue of one session in thebrana.

REPRODUCTION (twice, deliberately).
1. Submitted a merged payload with next[] length 10, containing two entries for t-2502: the prior close's text and a NEW, more accurate one (three reproductions, revised consensus fix). Written file came back with length 9 — the new entry was gone, the stale one kept. No warning, no error, ok:true.
2. Then submitted a payload with next[] length 9 where the single t-2502 entry's .text had been REPLACED with the new wording. Written file still shows the old text. Verified by grep: the marker string "THREE reproductions" is present in the submitted file and absent from the written file.

So the merge is not a dedup that keeps the last writer — it is a merge that PREFERS THE INCUMBENT. Consequence: once a next[] entry exists for a task_id, no later close that day can update its text. The field is effectively write-once-per-day-per-task_id.

WHY THIS MATTERS. next[] is the handoff — it is what the next session reads to decide what to do. An earlier close's understanding is frozen in, and a later close that learned the earlier guidance was WRONG cannot correct it. That is precisely what happened here: the first close said t-2502 was a clean "over-reach traded for under-reach"; by the second close that was known to be wrong (a third reproduction from another session showed over-reach still occurs), and the correction could not be written.

This also directly violates close/SKILL.md's own field note "Procedure decision points must never silently drop items" (2026-05-19) — the drop is in the CLI, below the procedure, so following the procedure correctly does not prevent it.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT. The 2026-05-19 field note on t-1461 covers replace-not-merge losing a PARALLEL session's data. This is the opposite defect in the fix for it: the merge added to prevent loss now prevents updates. Check whether t-1461's merge mode is where this incumbent-preference lives.

MITIGATION USED. The authoritative content was written to t-2502's context field instead, which is what the next session should trust over the handoff's next[] text. Note the handoff currently carries KNOWN-STALE guidance for t-2502.

AC: submitting an updated .text for an existing task_id in a same-day merge updates it
AC: if any incoming next[] entry is discarded or superseded, that is surfaced (warning/count), never silent
AC: decide and document the merge rule explicitly — last-writer-wins on text, union on distinct task_ids, and what happens for task_id: null entries
AC: regression test covering a same-day second write that changes the text of an existing task_id entry

2026-07-28 — REPRODUCED, with a more specific mechanism than this task's subject states.

SUBJECT SAYS: "session write discards updated next[] text" — i.e. framed as an UPDATE problem across two writes on the same day.
ACTUAL MECHANISM: `brana session write` deduplicates next[] BY task_id WITHIN A SINGLE WRITE. First entry for a given task_id wins; every subsequent entry carrying the same task_id is dropped. Silently — exit is {"ok":true}, no warning, no count in the response.

REPRO (live, this close, epic brana-v3-redesign):
  payload next[] = 10 entries
    3 entries with task_id "t-2488"
    1 each with "t-2502", "t-2495", "t-2506"
    4 entries with task_id null
  after write: 8 entries.
  Dropped: the 2nd and 3rd t-2488 entries. Kept: the 1st.
  All 4 null-task_id entries survived — null is NOT treated as a collision key.
  Re-wrote with the three t-2488 points folded into ONE entry: 8 in, 8 out, no loss.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE SUBJECT SUGGESTS. The dropped entries are not duplicates — they were three DIFFERENT follow-ups that happen to concern the same task. In this close the two dropped entries were the two open decisions the lane-identity ADR must settle (lane key = session-id vs branch vs task-id; and whether waves get populated or retired). Those are the highest-value items in the handoff, and they vanished with no signal. A handoff silently losing its own open questions is exactly the "procedure decision points must never silently drop items" rule in close/SKILL.md (2026-05-19 field note), violated at the storage layer instead of the procedure layer.

WORKAROUND until fixed: never emit more than one next[] entry per task_id in a single payload. Fold multiple points for one task into a single entry's text, or set task_id null (null entries are not deduped, at the cost of losing the task linkage).

FIX DIRECTION (not decided): either (a) stop deduping on task_id — the field is a REFERENCE, not a unique key, and several next steps legitimately share a task; or (b) if dedup is intentional, merge the texts rather than dropping, and report the count in the write response so the loss is at least visible. (a) looks correct: nothing about next[] semantics implies one-entry-per-task.

CLUSTER: this is the IDENTITY half of the concurrency cluster documented in docs/ideas/backlog-v3-lane-identity.md (with t-2502 and the sitrep ambiguity), NOT the atomicity half (t-2495). Fixing it does not require the lane-identity ADR to land first — the dedup is independently wrong and independently fixable, and it is arguably the cheapest real data-loss fix in the cluster.
2026-07-28 reproduced twice in one close, and the mechanism is now pinned more precisely:
(1) Two next[] entries sharing a task_id -> only the FIRST survives the write. Wrote 7 entries with two carrying task_id t-1781; 6 persisted, the second t-1781 entry vanished silently (no warning, exit 0).
(2) Re-writing the SAME task_id with corrected text does NOT update it — the original text is kept and the new text is discarded. Confirmed by diffing the persisted next[0].text against the payload on disk after a second `brana session write` in the same session.
(3) Entries with task_id: null do NOT dedup against each other — three null entries coexisted fine. So the dedup key is the non-null task_id, and null is exempt.
Practical consequence for the close procedure: any second follow-up for an already-referenced task must either be folded into that task's single entry, or filed with task_id: null. Both are workarounds around a silent data loss, not fixes.
Severity note: this silently drops handoff content at the exact moment it is meant to be preserved. The dropped item here was the merge instruction for a finished 6-commit branch.

2026-07-28 CHALLENGE-GATE FINDING — A SECOND CALL SITE. The fix must cover BOTH or it will regress:
  (1) dedup_next_items — brana-core/src/session.rs:123-134. Called from SessionState::sanitize() at session.rs:294, which runs on EVERY write path (session.rs:388, :391, :393). This is the one already reproduced.
  (2) merge_states — brana-core/src/session.rs:491-495. Implements the SAME task_id drop independently, on the same-day/same-branch merge path (reached from session.rs:366). That is the SECOND close of any given day — exactly when handoff volume is highest and when this bug was originally observed.
Fixing only dedup_next_items leaves merge_states dropping. Found by the ADR-069 challenge gate 2026-07-28; flagged there as a recurrence of the twin-fix-missed pattern.

DEPENDENCY NOTE (ADR-069 D2): merge_states is only reached when an existing file resolves at the same path. If lane keying moves to per-session filenames, the same-day merge branch stops firing and the t-2263 branch_has_active_worktree clobber guard (session.rs:377-388) becomes dead code. Fix this BEFORE the keying change so the fix is testable against live behaviour.
2026-07-28 (third close of the same session) — a FOURTH facet, and the one with no workaround at all: THERE IS NO WAY TO REMOVE A next[] ENTRY.

Sequence: an earlier close wrote {"task_id":"t-2512","text":"Fix validate.sh Check 29 on dev — ..."}. t-2512 was then investigated and CLOSED without any code change (the condition had already been fixed by another session). The handoff instruction is now actively wrong — it tells the next session to go regenerate a doc that is already current.

I could not update it (incumbent preference, documented above) and I could not delete it: `brana session write` unions incoming entries with existing ones, so omitting an entry from the payload does NOT remove it. Confirmed empirically — the final write carried 4 entries and the file came back with 11, the 5 incumbents included.

Only mitigation available was to ADD a null-task_id entry reading "SUPERSEDES the older t-2512 entry in this handoff — that entry is STALE and must be ignored". So the handoff now contains a wrong instruction followed some lines later by its own correction, and the wrong one sorts FIRST. A reader acting top-down hits the stale item before its retraction.

This makes next[] append-only in practice: entries can be added, never corrected, never withdrawn. For a field whose entire purpose is "what the next session should do", accumulating stale instructions with no retraction path is worse than losing an entry — a dropped item is invisible, a stale item is actively misleading.

Note the procedure has no escape hatch either: close/phases/session-state.md explicitly says "The LLM never writes session files directly — the CLI validates the schema and handles atomic writes + history archival", so hand-editing the JSON to drop the entry is out of bounds.

AC: a next[] entry can be removed — either by omission from a same-day payload, or via an explicit delete/replace mode on `brana session write`

AC: regression test — an entry present in the stored state and absent from a later same-day payload ends up absent (or is explicitly reported as retained, never silently)

2026-07-28 IMPLEMENTED — 3 commits on brana-v3-redesign/fix/t-2506-next-task-id-dedup, not yet merged.

MERGE RULE DECIDED (AC3/AC6): compare-and-swap, not a mode flag.
The caller passes the written_at it read as `base_written_at`.
  base matches stored -> REPLACE next[] (omitted entries removed, changed text lands)
  base stale          -> UNION + stderr warning (a concurrent write landed in between)
  base absent         -> UNION (caller never read, so omission cannot mean "remove")
accomplished[]/learnings[]/blockers[] union unconditionally — append-only logs of what
happened, whereas next[] is current forward-looking state and must be correctable.

WHY CAS AND NOT A next_mode FLAG: a flag asks the caller to ASSERT it read current state; a
caller that is wrong (or a procedure that drifts) then gets silent data loss. CAS detects the
actual hazard, so replace is unreachable without proof of a current read and the failure mode
is a redundant retention, never a silent loss.

2026-07-31 — DOWNSTREAM SYMPTOM, from a close that hit this bug and worked around it (originally filed as t-2578 defect 4; folded here).

The incumbent-preferring merge does not only block CORRECTING a next[] entry — it makes a close decline to WRITE one at all.

WHAT HAPPENED. The close filed two follow-up tasks (t-2576, t-2577) AFTER its session-state write had already landed. Attaching their ids meant a second same-day write. Knowing that a same-day merge is lossy — session_label combines with `|` and would self-append, and per this task the next[] text would not update anyway — the close DECLINED to write, and left both entries at `task_id: null`.

CONSEQUENCE, which is worse than the missing link. sitrep's task-ID staleness filter (sitrep/SKILL.md:130-135) suppresses next[] items whose task_id is completed or cancelled. An entry with `task_id: null` is unreachable by that filter, so it can never be suppressed — it resurfaces as an open follow-up on every future sitrep, forever, even after the work ships. Verified on the following session's sitrep, which rendered both as unlinked text under "Previous session next:".

So the merge semantics have a second-order effect on a DIFFERENT skill's staleness logic. A lossy same-day write teaches the writer not to write, and the un-written link then defeats the reader's garbage collection.

BEARING ON THE FIX. Whatever lands here should be checked against the "second close of the same day" flow end-to-end, not just against next[] text replacement:
  - session_label must be idempotent on re-write (or excluded from the merge), or closes will keep avoiding the second write for that reason alone.
  - a next[] entry whose task_id goes from null to a real id must be updatable, since that is exactly the correction this flow needs.
An alternative that sidesteps both: have close file its follow-up tasks BEFORE composing the state payload, so ids exist on the first write and no second write is needed. Cheaper than fixing the merge, but it does not fix the general case this task is about.

AC (additional): a close that files tasks after its first write can attach their ids without losing session_label or next[] text

tasks.description:
Close runs from the main checkout, but in repos using worktree-per-epic the session diff lives only on an epic integration branch that never touches main. Three surfaces read main and get the wrong answer.

(1) SNAPSHOT (Step 1b, ADR-052): the range is derived from main git log, so the queued diff for the nightly extraction cron contains only tasks.json + state files. Live 2026-07-28 proyecto_anita: an 858-line, 5-file change (t-2293) was entirely invisible to the cron; queued range 4ef86337..f2ece8a8 captured nothing of it.

(2) PROPAGATE L1 (Step 8b, ADR-056): the per-file loop guards on [ -f $f ], resolved against the main checkout. The only markdown the session touched (ADR-075) does not exist on main, so it was silently skipped and L1 reported PROPAGATE-L1: 0 gaps. Re-running the same checks inside the epic worktree gave a genuinely clean result — but the reported pass was vacuous, not earned. A vacuous clean bill of health is worse than no check.

(3) EPIC ACCUMULATOR (Step 9c): COMPLETED=$(git log --oneline -20 | grep -oE t-[0-9]+) sweeps main, which in a multi-session repo carries other epics commits. anita-envios tasks_completed now contains t-2250/2251/2252/2253/2285/2295/2305/2310/2311 (agent-memory, env-hardening and agent sessions) alongside its real ones, and inspection shows this has accreted over many prior closes, not just one.

Fix candidates: resolve the session branch/worktree first and anchor all three on it; or have close accept an explicit --branch/--worktree; or resolve per-file paths against the owning worktree in L1. Note (3) also needs a way to distinguish this sessions task IDs from co-committed ones — the ID grep over shared main is unsound regardless of which branch it reads.

Evidence: proyecto_anita close 2026-07-28, session-state-anita-envios.json, snap-20260728-131752.

tasks.description:
brana doctor reports: Hooks: 43/44 ok — missing: rtk" hook claude. The reported name contains a stray double-quote mid-string, which suggests doctor splits a hook command on quotes and treats a fragment as the hook name/path.

Evidence it is likely a false positive, not a real missing hook (2026-07-28, from a proyecto_anita close):
- the binary it names, ~/.local/bin/rtk, EXISTS and is executable (9.6M, mode 755)
- the literal string "hook claude" appears nowhere in ~/.claude/settings.json (0 matches)
- rtk references live in per-project .claude/settings.local.json (thebrana + proyecto_anita)

So the likely shape is a hook command such as "$HOME/.local/bin/rtk" hook claude ... whose quoted binary path defeats doctor name extraction, producing a bogus name that then fails an existence check.

NOT CONFIRMED — nobody verified the hook actually fires. Two outcomes possible: (a) doctor parsing bug, health is really 9/9; (b) the hook is genuinely mis-registered and doctor is right for the wrong reason. Confirm before fixing: locate the exact registration, run it manually, then either fix doctor extraction or fix the registration.

Low priority: it costs one perpetually-red doctor line, nothing functional observed.

tasks.description:
The session-start hook reported: Config drift detected (1 files). Re-run bootstrap.sh to sync: modified: rules/parallel-bash.md.

Investigated 2026-07-28 — there was no drift. ~/.claude/rules/parallel-bash.md is byte-identical to main:system/rules/parallel-bash.md. The newer, richer version (piped-exit-code is the filters, zsh $pipestatus vs bash PIPESTATUS, never pgrep -f in a wait loop, verify deploys by reading the deployed file) exists only on the dev branch, unpromoted.

So the check diffs the deployed copy against the WORKING TREE rather than against main. bootstrap deploys main -> live, so any unpromoted dev work is reported as drift by construction.

The loop is self-contradicting: the warning says re-run bootstrap.sh; bootstrap then refuses with ERROR: bootstrap deploys production (main -> live ~/.claude/). You are on dev. Promote to main first, or override: BRANA_BOOTSTRAP_FORCE=1. Following the prescribed remedy cannot resolve the warning, and the only way to make it go away is the override — which would deploy unpromoted dev state to live, exactly what the guard exists to prevent. That is a bad thing to nudge an operator toward every session start.

Fix: diff against main (or against the ref bootstrap would deploy), not the working tree. If diffing the working tree is intentional, the message must say unpromoted changes on {branch} — promote to main to deploy rather than re-run bootstrap.sh.

Separate, real, and NOT fixed by this task: the better guard guidance (; echo EXIT:$? over || true) is sitting unpromoted on dev, so every session is loading the weaker rule. Promoting dev -> main is a human decision, not part of this fix.

tasks.context:
Found 2026-07-28 running /brana:close --continue in thebrana.

MECHANISM. close/phases/session-state.md Step 9c builds the accumulator's completed-task list as:
  COMPLETED=$(git log --oneline -20 | grep -oE 't-[0-9]+' | sort -u | tr '\n' ',' | sed 's/,$//')
then passes it to `brana session epic upsert <slug> --completed "$COMPLETED"`.

That scrapes EVERY task ID mentioned in the last 20 commits on the current branch. On dev — a shared integration branch — those commits belong to other sessions. It does not check status, and it does not check whether this session touched the task.

OBSERVED. The close emitted:
  COMPLETED=t-1781,t-2398,t-2482,t-2488,t-2495,t-2496,t-2500,t-2501,t-2502,t-2503,t-2504,t-2505,t-2506,t-2507
Of those, t-2488 and t-2505 were in_progress at that moment (confirmed via `brana backlog query --status in_progress`), t-1781 was in_progress and deliberately left so by --continue, and t-2496 was cancelled, not completed. A "chore(tasks): file t-NNN" commit — i.e. a task being CREATED — reads identically to one being finished.

WHY IT MATTERS. The accumulator is what /brana:sitrep §4b loads for cross-day epic continuity. Poisoning it with false completions makes the next session believe finished work that is still open — the same class of wrong-state-at-resume that the handoff exists to prevent. It is silent: exit 0, {"ok":true}.

Note this is close's own scrape, distinct from t-2506 (session write's next[] dedup). Both silently corrupt handoff state, different layers.

FIX DIRECTION (not decided): filter the scraped IDs by actual status before passing them — only include ids whose backlog status is genuinely `completed`. Cheap and removes the whole class. Optionally also scope the log to the session range already computed in Step 1b (SESSION_RANGE) instead of a blind -20, so other sessions' commits are out of scope to begin with.

AC: the --completed list passed to `brana session epic upsert` contains only task IDs whose status is `completed`
AC: a task that is in_progress or cancelled and merely mentioned in a recent commit is never reported completed
AC: regression test covering a commit that mentions an in_progress task ID

tasks.context:
Found 2026-07-28 during t-2507 close — nearly shipped a false "validate passes" claim.

WHAT HAPPENED. Ran validate.sh via Bash run_in_background, redirecting output and appending its real status:
  ./validate.sh > LOG 2>&1; echo "VALIDATE_EXIT:$?" >> LOG
The harness task-notification then reported: `completed (exit code 0)`. The actual VALIDATE_EXIT recorded in the log was 1, with a FAIL line (Check 29, stale reference docs). The notification's 0 is the exit of the WRAPPER/compound command, not of validate.sh.

Only the explicitly recorded VALIDATE_EXIT caught it. Without that line the session would have reported a passing validate on a failing tree.

RELATIONSHIP TO THE EXISTING RULE. rules/parallel-bash.md already covers the sibling case ("A piped exit code is the filter's" — `./v.sh | tail; echo $?` reads 0) and notes $PIPESTATUS is bash-only while this harness is zsh. The background-wrapper case is the same family and is NOT covered: the signal comes from the harness notification rather than the shell, so it looks authoritative.

PROPOSED ADDITION (one line, same section):
  - **A background task's completion status is the wrapper's, not the command's.** Append `; echo "EXIT:$?" >> log` inside the backgrounded command and read that value; the notification's "exit code 0" says the wrapper ran, not that the work passed.

BLOCKER / SEQUENCING. rules/parallel-bash.md is always-loaded and the rule budget is saturated (t-2505 — 5 bytes headroom at last validate). This addition cannot land until that is resolved, so either sequence after t-2505 or land it as a field note in close/SKILL.md instead, where the trap actually bit.

AC: the trap is documented somewhere always-visible to a session running background validation
AC: if it lands in rules/parallel-bash.md, validate.sh's rule-budget check still passes

tasks.context:
Blocks all ADR-069 implementation. Three unverified assumptions, any of which can force redesign:
1) Does system/scripts/autonomous-runner.sh fire SessionStart inside its bubblewrap sandbox? If not, claude -p and cron runs get no lane pin, and D3b's 'missing pin -> fail loud' converts the whole autonomous surface from working-but-mis-attributed to NOT WORKING.
2) Does 'git worktree remove' delete the worktree's HEAD reflog? git-discipline MANDATES removal after merge, so D3.2's attribution evidence would be destroyed at exactly the moment close needs it. Direct collision between the ADR mechanism and the repo's own hard rule.
3) Does system/scripts/statusline-slow-cache.sh read session state? Unverified consumer; D1 makes read fail non-zero.
Raised by the 2026-07-28 challenge gate (3x RECONSIDER).

2026-07-28 ALL THREE ANSWERED — verified against source and, for Q2, empirically.

Q2 (worktree remove vs reflog) — CONFIRMED, and it is the one that bites.
`git worktree remove ../thebrana-t-2506` deleted `.git/worktrees/thebrana-t-2506/`
ENTIRELY, including `logs/HEAD`. Measured: 5 reflog entries before, admin dir and reflog
file both absent after. Commits survive (they were merged); only the per-lane attribution
evidence dies. Evidence preserved at scratchpad t2506-reflog-before.txt.

BUT THE ADR'S REASONING ABOUT THIS IS PARTLY WRONG, and the correction changes the fix.
ADR-069:266-268 says removal destroys the evidence "at exactly the moment close needs it."
That depends on an ordering the ADR does not state:
  close -> merge -> remove : reflog is LIVE at close. D3.2 works.
  merge -> remove -> close : reflog is GONE at close. D3.2 cannot attribute.
Both orderings happen. The second one happened in THIS session: t-2506 was merged to dev and
its worktree removed before close, so the three commits d332686c/cec60bf1/4158421b now have
no worktree reflog and fall back to the shared checkout's single reflog — which ADR-069 D3.2
itself says cannot attribute. So the mechanism is not unconditionally self-defeating; it is

2026-07-31 — LIVE REPRODUCTION of the D0 read/write key mismatch, during a /brana:close --continue on branch dev. Caught by the t-2506 CAS warning, which is exactly what made it visible.

WHAT HAPPENED. Step 9b says "read the base from the SAME key the write will use". I read the base from the orphan file (session-state.json, written_at 20:09:57Z) because branch=dev does not match the epic convention and a bare read resolves there. The write then routed to session-state-harness.json (written_at 21:14:24Z). Base mismatch -> CAS declined replace:

  next: {incoming:7, written:11, dropped_duplicates:0, retained_from_existing:4, mode:"union-stale-base"}
  WARNING: concurrent write detected — another session wrote at 21:14:24Z after you read.
           Unioned instead of replaced; 4 existing entries retained, nothing removed.

So a reader and a writer in the SAME process, one step apart, resolved two different keys. That is D0 stated as cheaply as it can be stated — no concurrency required to trigger it, only a branch that does not match the epic convention.

TWO FINDINGS BEYOND THE RESTATEMENT.

1. THE ORPHAN KEEPS THE STALE LIST, AND THAT IS WHAT dev READS. My handoff landed on the `harness` key; the orphan still holds the previous close's 6 entries, two of them now false (t-2571 is completed, and a "tasks.json left uncommitted" note whose tree is now clean). The next session on dev will bare-read the ORPHAN and get the stale list, not the fresh one. sitrep's staleness filter rescues the t-2571 entry (it has a task_id and can be suppressed) but not the null-id one. So the mismatch does not merely misfile a write — it splits the handoff in two, and the half that gets read is the older half.

2. REPLACE SEMANTICS ARE DANGEROUS ON A SHARED KEY — worth weighing before D2 lands. Of the 11 resulting entries, 4 belonged to a DIFFERENT lane (the harness lane's count-drift, spec-graph, PROPAGATE-candidate and t-2173-idle items). Had my base matched, replace would have REMOVED all four, silently, because omission-plus-valid-token means "withdraw". The CAS token authenticates that the writer read current state; it does not establish that the writer OWNS the entries it is omitting. On a per-lane key that distinction collapses and replace is safe. On a shared key it is a cross-lane clobber waiting for a base to happen to match — the union degradation is the only thing preventing it today.
   Implication for D2: per-lane keying is not just a correctness fix for reads, it is the PRECONDITION that makes t-2506's replace semantics safe to use at all. Shipping replace broadly before lane keys exist would trade a visible union-staleness problem for an invisible data-loss one.

NO WORKAROUND APPLIED, deliberately. Re-writing with the correct base would have replaced and taken the other lane's 4 entries with it. Union was accepted as the safe outcome. Recording this because "the warning fired and I did NOT retry" is the correct response and is not obvious from the warning text, which says "re-read and write again if you meant to withdraw an entry" — that advice is only safe when every entry on the key is yours.

2026-07-29 — D3.3's `dirty_at_start` PREDICATE HAS A HOLE, observed live during a close.

Sequence, in one close of the shared main checkout on dev:
  T0  gate check ran `git status --porcelain system/state/` -> EMPTY. system/state/ clean.
  T1  ~4 minutes later, after an unrelated `git add .claude/tasks.json && git commit`,
      `git status` showed system/scheduler/scheduler.template.json and system/state/scheduler.json
      STAGED (index column M) — a concurrent lane disabling the research-extraction job over a P0
      in personal-repo t-1366. Not this lane's work, and not staged by any hook (the pre-commit
      hook contains zero references to scheduler).

So a path can become foreign-dirty AND foreign-STAGED *mid-session*. `dirty_at_start` is a
snapshot taken before that happens, so the guard as specified would have seen a clean path and
allowed a commit that swept another lane's staged work. Nothing was lost here only because
`git add <explicit path>` does not unstage others and the commit happened to include just
tasks.json — verified: `git show --stat HEAD` listed one file. A `git add -A` would have swept it.

IMPLICATION: D3.3 needs the staged-set checked AT COMMIT TIME against "did this lane stage it",
not only against a lane-start dirty snapshot. Note the ADR already dropped the "and this lane
never wrote it" predicate as unknowable — but that reasoning was about WRITES to the working
tree. STAGING is different and IS observable: a lane knows which paths it ran `git add` on, so a
per-lane staged-path ledger is recordable without the write ledger D3 declined to build. That is
a narrower and achievable version of the dropped predicate.

Cheap partial mitigation available immediately, independent of D3.3: `git commit -a` is already
slated for rejection; extend the same treatment to a bare `git add -A`/`git add .` in the shared
checkout, which is the only way this particular sweep can happen accidentally.

tasks.context:
Found 2026-07-28 on the second /brana:close --continue of one session in thebrana.

MECHANISM. close/phases/gate-and-evidence.md CLOSE-ANCHOR-BLOCK computes the session window as:
  LAST_CLOSE = newest written_at across ALL session-state files (`brana session read --all`)
  COMMIT_COUNT = git log --since="$LAST_CLOSE" | wc -l
The `--all` was added by t-2491 to fix a REAL bug (an epic-routed close leaves session-state.json stale, so anchoring on the default file over-reaches). But `--all` sweeps every session file in the project, including those written by OTHER CONCURRENTLY-ACTIVE SESSIONS on unrelated epics.

OBSERVED. My close wrote session-state-knowledge-pipeline.json at 17:56:04Z. A concurrent lane (t-2488, ADR-069 decomposition) closed at 19:05:21Z. On my next close the anchor resolved to 19:05:21Z — a time AFTER all my work — so COMMIT_COUNT came back 0 and CHANGED_FILES was empty.

CONSEQUENCE (silent). With COMMIT_COUNT=0, Step 1b's close-snapshot.sh "exits silently without queueing" (its documented zero-commit behavior). The session's diff never reaches the nightly extraction cron. No warning, no error — the close reports success. This is the SAME failure the user flagged in this session's own opening handoff ("neither close snapshot captured it and tonight's extraction cron won't see it"), reached by a different route.

It also mis-fed close-classify.sh: an empty CHANGED_FILES with commit-count 0 classifies on no evidence.

I only caught it because the 0 looked wrong against work I knew I had done, and recomputed the range by hand from the previously-queued range end.

NOTE THE TENSION. Anchoring on the default file alone = t-2491's bug (over-reach on epic-routed closes). Anchoring on newest-across-all = this bug (under-reach under concurrency). Neither "pick one file" rule is correct; the anchor needs to be scoped to THIS session/lane, not to wall-clock newest.

FIX DIRECTION (not decided): anchor on the newest close belonging to this lane — the epic this close will route to (Step 9c's slug) or the current branch — rather than the global max. Alternative/simpler: anchor on the end of the last range this project QUEUED (close-queue already records git_range per project+branch), which is what I fell back to manually and is inherently per-lane.

Independently worth doing regardless of the anchor fix: make a zero-commit snapshot LOUD. "0 commits, nothing queued" should be surfaced in the close report, not silent — a close that queues nothing is either a genuine read-only session or a broken window, and those must not look identical.

AC: two sessions closing on the same project with different epics do not steal each other's anchor
AC: a close that queues nothing states so explicitly in its report
AC: regression test — session A closes, session B (different epic) closes later, session A closes again and its window still covers A's own commits

The warning is FALSE for this command. tasks.context:
Filed 2026-07-28 after backlog_add warned about the cap three times in one session and nothing changed as a result.

OBSERVED STATE. The cap is 10 open per epic. Actual: t-2338 cli-backlog-schema 50, t-2345 harness-core 39, t-2344 harness 14. The warning fires on every add ("epic t-NNNN is at its WIP cap (49/10 open) — adding this task makes 50; consider closing or parking before adding more") and the add proceeds regardless.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A DECISION RATHER THAN A CLEANUP. A limit breached 5x with no consequence is not a limit — it is a recurring line of output that trains everyone, human and agent, to ignore warnings from this tool. That is the actual cost: it degrades the signal value of every OTHER warning brana emits. I added three tasks to over-cap epics this session while dutifully reporting the warning each time, which is precisely the failure mode.

The v3 wave contract in t-2389 states "<=10 tasks/wave" as a design principle, so the number is not arbitrary — but nothing connects the principle to the enforcement.

THREE HONEST OPTIONS (pick one, do not leave it as-is):
1. ENFORCE — refuse the add over cap unless --force. Real teeth, but blocks capture-in-the-moment, which is how most of these tasks got filed. Risk: people stop filing tasks rather than start closing them.
2. RETIRE — drop the cap and the warning entirely; track WIP some other way (or not). Honest about how the backlog is actually used; loses the signal completely.
3. RESCOPE — cap "in_progress" rather than "open". Only 8 tasks are in_progress portfolio-wide, so a cap on in_progress would be meaningful, near-satisfied today, and would actually mean "how much am I juggling" rather than "how big is my inbox". This looks strongest: the current metric conflates backlog depth with work-in-flight, and only the latter is what WIP limits are for.

Whichever is chosen, the pre-work is the same: a parking pass on t-2338/t-2344/t-2345 to establish what is genuinely open vs. accumulated.

AC: a decision is recorded (enforce / retire / rescope) with its rationale
AC: the implementation matches the decision — no warning survives that has no consequence
AC: if rescoped to in_progress, the three named epics are re-measured under the new definition

Found 2026-07-28 at close of the t-2494 session. The rule reconcile-after-convention-change.md fired after a .claude/CLAUDE.md branch-convention edit, instructing `/brana:reconcile --scope propagation`. It is in ~/.claude/rules/, so it loads in EVERY project — but the command it prescribes is thebrana-shaped.

MEASURED SCOPE PORTABILITY (by path references in system/skills/reconcile/phases/*.md):

  scope          portable  why
  consistency    NO        hardcodes system/hooks, system/skills, system/rules, system/agents
                           vs docs/reflections, docs/architecture — thebrana's post-ADR-006
                           layout. No client repo has system/.
  propagation    NO        PROP-1 shells `bash system/scripts/verify-docs.sh` (thebrana path).
                           PROP-2 is gated on `docs/spec-graph.json` exists, so it degrades
                           quietly — but PROP-1 does not.
  security       NO        8 refs to system/agents, system/hooks, system/skills, ~/.claude/rules.
                           Audits the brana system itself, not a client application.
  knowledge      YES       0 system/ refs; only ~/.claude/projects (machine-global).

The skill header states it outright: "Unified maintenance command for the brana system." consistency is the DEFAULT scope, so a bare `/brana:reconcile` in a client repo is the least portable form.

WHY THIS IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN REMEMBERING. The failure is silent-clean, not loud. In a client repo the propagation scope either errors on a missing script or finds nothing and reports no drift — and "no drift found" is indistinguishable from "never actually checked this repo's docs". That is the exit-code-is-not-evidence-of-work class applied to a maintenance command: a check that cannot fail is not a check. Anyone trusting a clean reconcile result in a client repo is trusting nothing.

VERIFICATION GAP IN THIS FILING — READ BEFORE ACTING. The portability table above is derived from PATH REFERENCES ONLY. reconcile was NOT actually run in a non-thebrana repo. The hardcoded paths are certain; the runtime failure mode is not — consistency and security may degrade gracefully rather than erroring. Establish which it is FIRST, because it decides the fix: a loud failure needs only a guard, a silent-clean pass needs the guard AND a correction to anything that previously reported clean.

LIKELY FIX (pick after the above is settled):
1. Scope the rule — add a `paths:` predicate or an explicit "thebrana only" precondition so it stops firing in client repos. Cheapest, and it removes the false signal at the source.
2. Guard the skill — reconcile detects a missing system/ and refuses loudly instead of no-opping. Fixes every caller, not just this rule.
3. Both. Option 2 alone still leaves the rule instructing users to run something that will refuse.

Prefer 2 at minimum: the rule is only one caller, and any future rule or habit pointing at reconcile inherits the same trap.

BROADER SWEEP WORTH DOING WITH THIS: reconcile-after-convention-change is unlikely to be the only global rule prescribing a thebrana-only command. Audit ~/.claude/rules/ for other rules naming brana skills, system/ paths, or repo-specific scripts, and classify each as global / thebrana-only. delegation-routing.md and retrieval-routing.md both name brana-specific surfaces and are worth checking first.

AC: it is established whether reconcile fails loudly or passes silent-clean outside thebrana, and that finding is recorded
AC: running the prescribed command in a non-thebrana repo either works or refuses with a clear reason — never reports a clean result it did not verify
AC: ~/.claude/rules/ audited for other rules prescribing thebrana-only commands; each classified global or thebrana-only
AC: reconcile-after-convention-change.md no longer fires unqualified in projects where its command cannot run

tasks.context:
Filed 2026-07-28, immediately after t-2535 shipped — and it questions t-2535's premise rather than extending it. Operator's framing: "this is the mechanism you have just built. maybe we need to rethink it."

THE PROBLEM. t-2535 changed WHICH tasks the WIP cap counts (open -> live, excluding parked). It did not touch WHERE the count comes from: self-reported fields on the task (status, tags). Measured the same day, three signals for "what is in flight" disagree with each other and none is authoritative:

  signal                      count            what it actually measures
  WIP cap (post-t-2535)       47 / 14 / 39     backlog depth per epic (t-2338/t-2344/t-2345)
  status:in_progress          7                self-reported, portfolio-wide
  live git worktrees          6                work someone actually started

CONCRETE DIVERGENCES (all verified 2026-07-28, not inferred):
- thebrana-t2138 worktree exists; t-2138 status is COMPLETED. Worktree has outlived its task since 2026-06-19 (~6 weeks).
- t-2173: worktree is on branch orbit/feat/t-2173-egress-allowlist; the task's `branch` FIELD says orbit/feat/t-2173-sandbox-executor. The field and the repo name different branches.
- t-2492 has a live worktree (harness-core/fix/t-2492-ci-test-suite); its task `branch` field is null.
- t-2214 and t-2249 are status:in_progress with branch null and no worktree at all.
- t-2173 is in_progress with its last commit 2026-06-22 — 5 weeks idle, indistinguishable from active by status alone.

So of 6 worktrees: 1 belongs to a completed task, 1 disagrees with its task's branch field, 1 is absent from its task's branch field, and 1 has been idle 5 weeks. Of 7 in_progress tasks, 3 have no branch.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE PREDICATE FIX. t-2535's whole argument was that the cap should measure work-in-flight rather than inbox depth. But `status:in_progress` is NOT work-in-flight either — it is a field someone remembered to set, and the evidence above shows it is not maintained. Had t-2535 rescoped to in_progress as originally decided, the cap would have read 7 portfolio-wide while 6 worktrees sat open, 1 of them orphaned. Fixing the predicate over an unreliable input yields a precise number that is still wrong.

GROUND TRUTH CANDIDATES (worktrees/branches/commit recency) are observable rather than declared — nobody has to remember to update them. That is the property the current inputs lack.

QUESTIONS TO SETTLE (this is research/design, not a code task):
1. Should WIP be DERIVED (worktree + branch + commit recency) rather than declared? Derived cannot drift, but it misses work not yet branched — capture-in-the-moment tasks, research, anything done in the main checkout.
2. If derived, what is the reconciliation surface when field and repo disagree — does the repo win silently, or does it fail loud? (feedback_verify-existence-checks and pattern_exit-code-is-not-evidence-of-work both argue loud.)
3. Is a stale-worktree sweep a recurring check (validate.sh / session-end-drift) or a manual command? Note the 6-week-old orphan was found by eye, not by any check.
4. Does this subsume or replace the WIP cap entirely? An epic's real WIP might be "worktrees whose branch names carry this epic's slug" — which the branch convention already encodes, and which t-2540's epic-segment ruling would make reliable or not.

DEPENDENCY: t-2540 (is the {epic-slug}/ branch segment mandatory?) gates option 4 — deriving epic WIP from branch names only works if the epic segment is guaranteed present.

AC: the three signals are reconciled into one documented definition of "in flight", or an explicit decision recorded that they measure different things on purpose
AC: field-vs-repo disagreement has a defined resolution that does not silently prefer the stale side
AC: orphaned worktrees (task completed/cancelled, worktree alive) are detectable by a check rather than by eye
AC: it is decided whether the WIP cap keeps its current input or moves to a derived one

2026-07-28 — MEASURED. Full reconciliation of the three signals (script: scratchpad/wip-inventory.sh; re-runnable).

WORKTREE INVENTORY (6 worktrees, excl. main checkout):
  worktree              branch                                        task     status       idle  divergence
  thebrana-orbit-t2173  orbit/feat/t-2173-egress-allowlist            t-2173   in_progress  36d   FIELD-MISMATCH (field says orbit/feat/t-2173-sandbox-executor) + IDLE
  thebrana-t-1781       knowledge-pipeline/feat/t-1781-...            t-1781   in_progress   0d   clean
  thebrana-t2138        harness/feat/t-2138-secret-scan-hook          t-2138   COMPLETED    38d   ORPHAN + field null + idle
  thebrana-t2443        skills/fix/t-2443-suggest-core-skill-filter   t-2443   in_progress   4d   clean
  thebrana-t2492        harness-core/fix/t-2492-ci-test-suite         t-2492   in_progress   0d   field null
  thebrana-t2542        cli-backlog-schema/fix/t-2542-branch-guard... t-2542   pending       0d   field null + status never set

DECLARED-BUT-NOT-STARTED (in_progress, no worktree): t-2214 (branch null), t-2249 (branch set, no worktree), t-2541.

HEADLINE: ONLY 2 OF 6 WORKTREES (33%) FULLY AGREE WITH THEIR TASK RECORD. Counts: 6 worktrees vs 7 in_progress, overlapping on only 4.

THE DECISIVE DATUM — I PRODUCED A FRESH DIVERGENCE WHILE MEASURING THIS ONE. t-2542's worktree was cut during this session; I never set its status or branch field, so the inventory flagged my own hour-old task as pending-with-a-live-worktree. This is not historical sloppiness from other lanes: it is what declared state does under ordinary, attentive use, by someone actively working on the drift problem. Any argument that the fields would be reliable 'if people were careful' is falsified by the person who filed the task.

DIRECTION OF ERROR IS ONE-WAY: in every one of the 4 divergences the repo was correct and the field was stale, absent, or naming a branch that does not exist. No case found where the field was right and the repo wrong. That asymmetry is the argument for deriving: worktree/branch/commit-date are OBSERVED, and nobody has to remember to update an observation.

NO DETECTION EXISTS TODAY: grepped validate.sh (67 checks) and system/hooks/session-end-drift.sh — zero references to worktree staleness or orphan detection. The 38-day orphan was found by eye while listing worktrees for an unrelated reason.

Q4 IS NOW ANSWERABLE (was gated on t-2540, completed 2026-07-28): the epic segment is MANDATORY with no fallback, and t-2542 makes branch-name-warn.sh enforce it on 'git worktree add -b' — the path git-discipline.md mandates. So going forward every worktree branch is guaranteed to carry a parseable {epic-slug}. Deriving per-epic WIP from worktree branch names is therefore mechanically possible for NEW branches. CAVEAT: the 6 existing worktrees predate the guard, though all 6 happen to conform.


DECISIONS (operator, 2026-07-28):
Q1 — DERIVED, WITH DECLARED AS FALLBACK. Worktree + branch + commit recency are authoritative for 'in flight'. The task field becomes a cache to be corrected, not trusted. Declared state is retained ONLY to cover work that has no branch yet (capture-in-the-moment, research, main-checkout edits) — deriving alone would make such work structurally uncountable, including t-2541 itself. Two ranked signals, not one.
Q2 — FAIL LOUD, NEVER AUTO-CORRECT. Disagreement is reported and requires human resolution. Rationale: matches this repo's own precedent (pattern_exit-code-is-not-evidence-of-work; close/phases/session-state.md:237 'lookup failures are not negatives', t-2487). Decisive concrete argument: a silent auto-fix would have rewritten t-2173's branch field to match the repo and DESTROYED the evidence that the two had diverged for 36 days. Auto-correct is right in all 4 observed cases and still wrong, because it erases the drift rate.
Q3 — validate.sh CHECK. A new check alongside the existing 67, failing loud on the surface already trusted for green/red. The 38-day t-2138 orphan would have been caught 38 days ago. Rejected session-end-drift as the primary site per rules-over-hooks-for-gates.md.


Q4 / AC4 — KEEP THE CAP AS-IS; ADD DERIVED WIP AS A SEPARATE MEASURE (operator, 2026-07-28).
The WIP cap remains anti-sprawl over live children — exactly what t-2535 shipped and what backlog-v3-schema.md §72 specifies. A derived in-flight count becomes a DISTINCT measure surfaced in validate/sitrep, not folded into the cap.
RATIONALE: backlog depth and work-in-flight are different quantities, and merging them into one number is the same mistake t-1340 fixed (raw vs synthetic conflated in one map until neither could be reproduced). Keeping them separate also means nothing built today is reverted, and the add-path keeps a single warning rather than two — t-2535 was filed to reduce warning noise, not add to it.
NOTE: a derived cap would also be structurally awkward at add-time, since a task being added has no branch yet.

ALL FOUR ACs NOW SATISFIED. t-2541 is complete as a design task; implementation spins out separately.

tasks.context:
Found 2026-07-28 while answering t-2516 G2. Searched the backlog first — zero existing tasks on this.

MECHANISM (verified against source, system/scripts/autonomous-runner.sh:80-103). sandbox_claude()
runs `claude -p` under bubblewrap with `--tmpfs /home`, bind-mounting exactly three things
beneath it: ~/.cargo, ~/.gitconfig, ~/.claude/.credentials.json. `~/.claude/projects/` is NOT
mounted. So find_project_root()'s store path resolves inside the tmpfs: session state can be
neither read nor written durably, and whatever is written dies with the jail. settings.json and
hooks/ are also unmounted and the process runs under `env -i`, so SessionStart cannot fire
either (that half is recorded on t-2516 and t-2521).

WHY THIS IS NOT OBVIOUSLY A BUG — and why it needs a ruling rather than a fix:
- The runner HAS its own record: emit() appends {id,subject,decision,reason,ts} to
  $RUNNER_LEDGER (autonomous-runner.sh:108). But that is a DISPATCH ledger — it records whether
  a task was taken and why it was excluded, not what happened during the work.
- ADR-062 (the sandbox decision) does not mention session state, handoffs, or projects/ at all
  (grepped). So this is an unexamined consequence of the mount list, not a documented decision.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY LOST: learnings[] and next[] from autonomous work. A later session reading the
handoff store sees nothing from any autonomous run, and cannot tell that work happened.

TWO ADMISSIBLE OUTCOMES:
1. Deliberate — autonomous runs are not handoff-producing lanes. Then say so in ADR-062, and
   ADR-069 D3b must stop assuming the autonomous surface carries a lane pin at all.
2. Defect — then either bind-mount the store into the jail (widens the write surface the
   sandbox exists to narrow — ADR-062 tradeoff), or have the runner write the handoff
   HOST-SIDE after the jail exits, from the ledger plus the worktree's commits. The host-side
   option preserves the sandbox's containment and is the likely answer if it is a defect.

INTERACTION WITH t-2521 (D0+D1+D2): a lane pin alone does not make the autonomous surface work,
because there is no durable store inside the jail to pin TO. Whichever way this is ruled,
t-2521's "lane init on the host vs bind-mount the store" choice depends on it. Not blocking
t-2521 — but t-2521 should not be implemented as if a sandboxed run can write state.

CAUTION: verify against the CURRENT mount list before acting; autonomous-runner.sh is actively
edited and the bind list at :92-100 is the authority, not this note.

THE GAP. `system/` is the source; `~/.claude/` is what actually runs (hooks, rules, agents — the bootstrap.sh identity layer). Merging to dev changes the source and nothing else. There is no signal anywhere that the running copy is behind, so a fix reads as 'done, merged, green' while the defect it fixes is still live.

MEASURED 2026-07-28 (diff -rq system/<dir> vs ~/.claude/<dir>):
  hooks:  3 differing/missing entries
  rules:  1
  agents: 0
Small surface, but the 3 hook entries include t-2542's branch-name-warn.sh fix, merged and closed minutes earlier. So right now: kind:design branches are still rejected and `git worktree add -b` is still unvalidated, on a task marked completed with a green validate.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME FAILURE CLASS THIS BACKLOG KEEPS HITTING. It is exit-code-is-not-evidence-of-work at the deploy boundary: every signal we DO check (tests green, validate PASSED, task completed, branch merged) is true, and none of them means the change is in force. Compare t-2535 (a warning with no consequence), ADR-069's fail-open, and t-2536 (a maintenance command that reports clean without checking). A green that does not imply the thing works is the recurring shape.

SECOND-ORDER RISK: because nothing surfaces the gap, the natural correction is 'run bootstrap.sh more often' — but bootstrap deploys the WHOLE identity layer, so an ad-hoc run also ships every other lane's unmerged-to-main work sitting in the tree. Deploy granularity is part of the problem, not just deploy frequency. See the sibling ship-cadence task.

SCOPE — AUDIT, DIAGNOSE, IMPROVE:
1. AUDIT: enumerate exactly which paths bootstrap.sh copies into ~/.claude/ vs which are plugin-loaded from system/ (CLAUDE.md says skills load via plugin, hooks/rules/agents via bootstrap — verify, do not assume). The answer determines which files can even drift.
2. DIAGNOSE: for each drifting file today, establish whether it is undeployed-new, hand-edited-live (which the 'never edit ~/.claude/ directly' rule forbids), or an artefact of plugin-vs-bootstrap split.
3. IMPROVE: a check that reports repo-vs-live drift. Fail-loud, consistent with t-2541's ruling — never silently rsync, because a silent sync would deploy whatever else is in the tree.

OPEN QUESTION FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS: should the check be red (blocking) or informational? A merged-but-undeployed fix is a normal intermediate state between merge and ship, so blocking on it would make dev permanently red. Likely a distinct 'deploy pending' report rather than a validate failure — decide before implementing.

INSTANCE. t-2506 (next[] dedup + CAS) merged to dev 2026-07-28. At the close that immediately
followed, `brana session write` submitted 13 next[] entries and 12 landed — the silently dropped
one being the second entry sharing task_id t-2524, which was the finding discovered during that
very close. Exit 0, {"ok":true}, no warning. The fix for exactly this bug was sitting in dev,
merged and tested (1265 passing), and inert. So repo-vs-live drift is not only "a fix is not yet
in force" — it actively corrupted the handoff whose job was to report the fix.

SECOND DRIFT CHANNEL — bootstrap.sh is NOT sufficient. This task's framing ("invisible until
bootstrap.sh runs") covers system/ → ~/.claude/. But `brana` is a COMPILED BINARY at
~/.local/bin/brana, installed by a separate step, and bootstrap.sh does not rebuild it.
Verified: the live binary was built Jul 27 and `strings ~/.local/bin/brana | grep -c
base_written_at` returns 0, i.e. it has no knowledge of a field added the next day. So there are

  1. system/ → ~/.claude/        (bootstrap.sh)
  2. system/cli/rust → ~/.local/bin/brana  (cargo build + install)

the binary silently ate handoff entries. Whatever check this task produces must cover both, and

Filed 2026-07-28. This is a diagnosis task about the ship process, NOT a request to ship — do not resolve it by running the merge.

THE LOOP, EVIDENCED. t-2214 ('Ship dev→main + bootstrap.sh') was filed 2026-06-21 and DEFERRED THE SAME DAY. Its own recorded reason: 'Al evaluar, dev creció a 83 commits (no solo scaffolder t-2213)'. It was deferred BECAUSE the batch had grown — and the batch grows precisely while it is deferred. Five weeks later it is still status:in_progress, started:null, branch:null, effort S, and dev is 55 commits ahead of main again.

So the failure is not neglect. Deferring was locally reasonable each time: a large undifferentiated batch is genuinely riskier to promote than a small one. The process makes the safe local choice compound into the unsafe global state.

MEASURED 2026-07-28 (verify before trusting — these move fast):
- main tip: bef34d56, authored ~2h before filing. A ship DID happen today, so this is not a stalled-forever situation; it is a batch that re-accumulates faster than it drains.
- dev: 55 commits ahead of main, from at least 4 concurrent lanes merging in the same session.
- t-2214 is itself one of the 'declared but not started' entries t-2541 flagged: in_progress, no branch, no worktree. The task for shipping shows the same drift as the work it would ship.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. Nothing in system/ is in force until ship (see sibling task on repo-vs-live drift). So ship latency is the latency on EVERY hook, rule and agent fix — t-2542's branch-guard fix included. The longer the batch, the longer every fix in it stays inert, which raises the stakes of each promotion and makes the next deferral more likely.

ALSO NOTE — a stale handoff claimed 'DEPLOY PENDING — dev is 12 commits ahead of main'. That number was wrong when written (dev was 1 ahead) and wrong later (10, then 16, then 55). A deploy-pending signal that nobody can trust is worse than none, because it is indistinguishable from a verified one. Any fix here should make the count derived at read time, not written into a handoff.

QUESTIONS TO ANSWER (this is research/design):
1. Is ff-only promotion of a 55-commit batch actually riskier than 5 batches of 11? Name the concrete risk — is it review burden, rollback granularity, bootstrap blast radius, or in-flight session breakage (t-2214's own note says 'Reiniciar sesiones en vuelo tras el deploy')?
2. Should ship be time-triggered (e.g. at close, if dev is ahead), size-triggered (ship at N commits before it compounds), or event-triggered (any hook/rule change ships immediately, since those are inert until deployed)?
3. Does the two-tier model (ADR-060) still hold if the buffer never drains? A permanent buffer is a third branch, not an integration point.
4. What is the actual cost of a bad promotion — is `git revert` on main plus re-bootstrap sufficient, or is rollback genuinely hard? The whole deferral instinct rests on this being expensive, and nobody has measured it.

AC: the real risk of promoting a large batch is named and, if possible, measured — including rollback cost
AC: a trigger rule for ship is decided (time / size / event) with rationale
AC: any deploy-pending indicator is derived at read time, never a written-down count that can go stale

2026-07-31 — MEASURED. All four questions answered with numbers. The deferral premise does not survive measurement.

BATCH SIZE, AND ITS GROWTH RATE:
  dev ahead of main: 68 commits (this task's context recorded 55 on 2026-07-28 -> +13 in 3 days)
  main ahead of dev: 0 -> `git merge --ff-only dev` works today, verified via merge-base --is-ancestor
  oldest undeployed commit: 9129bd5c, 2026-07-24 (7 days)
  total diff: 48 files changed, 4534 insertions, 269 deletions

Q1 — IS A 68-COMMIT BATCH RISKIER THAN 6 BATCHES OF 11? NO, AND THE QUESTION IS MIS-FRAMED.
Commit count is the wrong risk metric, and it is the metric driving deferral. Blast radius by
deploy surface across main..dev:
  system/hooks    3 files   (3 commits)   <- bootstrap channel, INERT until deploy
  system/rules    0 files
  system/agents   0 files
  system/skills   3 files                 <- plugin channel
  system/cli     10 files  (16 commits)   <- binary channel, separate install
  docs           26 files                 <- deploys NOTHING, live in repo on merge
  .claude         1 file   (tasks.json)   <- deploys nothing
So 68 commits reduce to SIX deploy-relevant files plus a binary rebuild. The number that
looks alarming is dominated by docs and task-record churn that has no deployed footprint at
all. Deferring a promotion because "it grew to 68" is deferring on a figure uncorrelated with
what could break.

Q4 — WHAT DOES A BAD PROMOTION ACTUALLY COST? LOW, AND MEASURABLE.
  - ff-only means main simply moves. There is no merge commit to unwind; rollback is moving
    the ref back.
  - bootstrap.sh deploys hooks with `rsync -a --delete` (bootstrap.sh:405,417) — a MIRROR, not
    an accumulation. Re-running it from an earlier checkout restores the earlier state exactly.
    Rollback is deterministic, not lossy.
  - bootstrap.sh:395 already has `--dry-run --itemize-changes` for the hooks surface, so the
    blast radius is inspectable BEFORE deploying. The tool to de-risk this already exists and
    is not being used as a decision input.
  - EXCEPTION: bootstrap.sh does NOT rebuild the brana binary (no cargo build/install; it only
    symlinks brana-scheduler at :684). Rolling back the binary is a separate cargo step.
The deferral instinct rests on rollback being expensive. Measured, it is one ref move plus an
idempotent mirror re-run. Nobody had measured it; that is why the instinct persisted.

WHAT IS INERT RIGHT NOW, RE-MEASURED:
  diff -rq system/<dir> vs ~/.claude/<dir>:  hooks 3 differing, rules 1, agents 0
    -> UNCHANGED from t-2546's 2026-07-28 measurement. Three days, no movement.
  live binary: built 2026-07-27T20:30; newest system/cli commit 2026-07-29T10:26 (4 days stale)
  `strings ~/.local/bin/brana | grep -c base_written_at` = 0
    -> t-2506's CAS fix is confirmed ABSENT from the running binary. Every close today still
       silently drops next[] entries, with the fix merged, tested and inert.
The two named inert commits are still inert: f6a736c6 (t-2542 branch guard) and cec60bf1
(t-2506 CAS).

Q2 — TRIGGER: EVENT, NOT TIME OR SIZE. Rationale from the above:
Size-triggered is disqualified — it triggers on the metric Q1 shows is uncorrelated with risk,
and would fire constantly on docs churn while a single inert hook fix waited.
Time-triggered treats a doc commit and a hook commit as equally urgent; they are not. A doc
commit is LIVE the moment it merges. A hook/rule/agent commit is DEAD until bootstrap runs.
Event-triggered follows the actual failure mode: ship when the deploy surface changes.
  PROPOSED RULE: any commit touching system/hooks, system/rules, system/agents, or system/cli
  ships on merge. Everything else (docs, tasks.json, reviews) rides along at no extra cost —
  ff-only means there is no partial promotion anyway.
Under this rule the current batch would have shipped on 2026-07-28 with f6a736c6, and t-2506's
data loss would not have occurred.

Q3 — DEPLOY-PENDING INDICATOR, DERIVED AT READ TIME. The stale-handoff number this task
criticises (12, then 1, 10, 16, 55, now 68) was wrong because it counted COMMITS. The derived
indicator should count the DEPLOY SURFACE, which is small, stable and actionable:
  git diff --name-only main..dev -- system/hooks system/rules system/agents system/cli | wc -l
plus a binary staleness check (live mtime vs newest system/cli commit). Today that reads
"13 deploy-relevant files + binary 4 days stale" rather than "68 commits", and the first is a
number someone can act on.

AC5 — t-2214 IS ALREADY `cancelled` (verified 2026-07-31). Resolved independently; no action.

STILL OPEN, NOT DECIDED HERE: whether the event trigger is enforced by a hook, a close step,
or convention. Deciding the rule was this task's contract; enforcing it is implementation and
should be a separate task so this one can close. NOTE the enforcement choice matters more than
usual here — an unenforced ship rule is exactly the advisory-signal class (t-2561, ADR-065 D4)
this backlog keeps rediscovering.

tasks.description:
Found from proyecto_anita during a /brana:close --continue on 2026-07-28. The deployed CLI does NOT implement two behaviours that system/skills/close/phases/session-state.md documents as landed in t-2506. Both fail SILENTLY — the write returns {"ok":true,"path":...} with no indication.

GAP 1 — base_written_at CAS is ignored; next[] always unions.
The phase doc (Step 9b) says a same-day write with a matching base_written_at REPLACES next[], and that omitting an item + passing the token is how you withdraw it. Reality: base_written_at is not read at all (it is not in `brana session write --help`, which offers only --file and --minimal). Every write unions, so a next[] entry can be ADDED but never corrected and never withdrawn.
The doc also specifies a response block reporting what landed — {"next":{"incoming":N,"written":N,"dropped_duplicates":N,"retained_from_existing":N,"mode":"replace|union|union-stale-base"}} — and says a `union-stale-base` mode plus a stderr warning is how the concurrency downgrade is announced. None of that is emitted. There is no way for a caller to detect the downgrade.

GAP 2 — task_id is still a dedup key, and the INCUMBENT text wins.
The doc states explicitly: 'Dedup key: next[] entries are deduplicated by case-folded trimmed text only. task_id does not participate.' It carries a historical note saying task_id USED to be a dedup key and that the incumbent text won. That historical behaviour is the CURRENT behaviour. Submitting an updated text for an existing task_id silently discards the update and keeps the older text.

EVIDENCE (live, proyecto_anita agent epic, 2026-07-28):
Submitted a curated 21-item next[] with base_written_at set to the file's exact written_at (2026-07-28T20:52:13.659750834+00:00). Result: 43 items on disk (33 prior + 21 mine, minus 11 identical-text collapses). Every item intended for withdrawal survived. MEASURED 2026-07-29 on dev (re-verify, this moves):
  git status --porcelain docs/spec-graph.json -> ` M docs/spec-graph.json`
  git diff --stat -> 124 insertions, 3 deletions, unstaged
  git log --oneline -- docs/spec-graph.json shows the pattern plainly — it is regenerated as a
  TRAILING chore by whichever task happened to notice:
    0c5c0202 chore(graph): regenerate spec-graph — pick up check-adr-uniqueness.sh (t-2515)
    ef4e8581 chore(graph): regenerate spec-graph after ADR renumbering (t-2507)
    06e3dd85 chore(graph): regenerate spec-graph after ADR-069 and context-budget landings
  Three separate lanes each cleaning up after themselves, none owning the file.

WHY THIS IS A REAL PROBLEM AND NOT TIDINESS. It is a generated artifact tracked in git with no
regeneration trigger, so it is dirty by default and its dirtiness carries no information. Two
concrete harms:

1. IT POISONS THE STAGING GUARD WORK. t-2524's D3.3 guard rejects staging paths that were dirty
   at lane start. A file that is ALWAYS dirty and belongs to no lane is exactly the input that
   forces operators into `--adopt-path` habitually — and a guard that is routinely overridden
   stops being a guard. Related: the D3.3 hole recorded on t-2524 the same day (system/state/
   went foreign-STAGED four minutes after a clean gate) is the same shape — shared generated
   state with no owner.

2. IT IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM REAL DRIFT. Consumers treat this file as truth: validate.sh
   Check 14 (undocumented system/ files), /brana:close Step 6 doc-drift detection (t-397),
   /brana:build blast-radius (t-349), LOAD graph traversal (t-934), session-start staleness
   (t-351). All of them read a file that is habitually 124 lines behind the tree. A stale graph
   makes every one of those report a clean or incomplete answer it did not verify —
   exit-code-is-not-evidence-of-work, applied to a cache.

QUESTIONS TO SETTLE BEFORE CODING (this is a small decision task, not a big build):
- Should it be tracked at all? Gitignoring it and generating on demand removes the dirty-by-
  default problem entirely, at the cost of a build step for every consumer and losing history.
  Note t-2223 (universal doc graph) argues for DERIVED-not-declared as the lean direction and
  explicitly says derive kills staleness — check that before choosing to keep it committed.
- If it stays tracked, what regenerates it and when? Candidates: a close step, a pre-commit hook
  when docs/ or system/ changed, or a validate check that FAILS on staleness rather than a
  chore commit someone remembers.
- Who commits it — the lane that dirtied it (needs the graph build to be cheap and deterministic
  so two lanes do not produce conflicting output) or a dedicated maintenance pass?

DETERMINISM IS A PREREQUISITE, CHECK IT FIRST: if `brana graph build` output is not byte-stable
for the same input, then any per-lane regeneration turns into a merge-conflict generator and only
the single-owner option works. Establish this before deciding.

AC: a decision recorded on tracked-vs-generated, with the t-2223 derived-not-declared direction explicitly considered

AUDIT 2026-07-29. Root cause of a five-defect chain in the telegram link-capture pipeline (personal repo t-1363/1364/1365/1366/1367). Full diagnosis:

1. SUCCESS IS DEFINED AS EXIT STATUS, everywhere. research-extraction.sh does `if claude -p ... >/dev/null 2>&1; then brana backlog set $id status completed`. /brana:research exits 0 without writing an artifact (its procedure is built around brana-knowledge dimension docs + research-sources.yaml + scout subagents, none of which apply to a bare link task), so links drained into completed with nothing stored. That is personal-repo t-1366 (P0).

2. THE TEST SUITE CERTIFIES THE BUG. deploy/test-research-extraction.sh passes 8/8. Its claude stub is 3 lines ending in `exit 0`, and the test "one pending task: marked completed after successful research" asserts exactly the P0 behaviour. The suite can never catch t-1366 because it encodes it as the spec.

3. THE STUB DOESN'T READ STDIN; the real claude -p does. research-extraction.sh calls claude inside a `while read` loop fed by a heredoc, so the real binary drains the remaining ids: the batch truncates to 1 and the swallowed ids leak into the prompt. Why Rust rather than patching the bash: the shell loop/stdin hazard becomes structurally impossible, and the code lands inside validate.sh + the existing 1188-test suites. The bash script lives in personal/deploy/, outside every check thebrana runs, which is why defects 3, 4 and 5 shipped consecutively with 18 green tests on disk.

- `is_cancellable(outcome)` (knowledge.rs:118) already gates on the artifact: Store|AlreadyStored => true; NotFound|EmptyContent => false, with the comment "a miss or an empty fetch leaves the link genuinely unread, so cancelling its stub would silently drop the work".

2. Run the existing batch path, then mark completed ONLY where is_cancellable(outcome) is true.

THIS IS THE EXACT DIVERGENCE THE CHALLENGE REVIEW PREDICTED. docs/reviews/backlog-v3-schema-challenge-2026-07-20.md item 4 rated it CRITICAL -> WARNING [VERIFIED]: "active_epic promoted to load-bearing while live-divergent at review time (global copy named a non-thebrana epic; project-local copy absent -> WIP cap would silently no-op; t-1883 guard is sync-time only)". THE UNIMPLEMENTED REMEDY IS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN. backlog-v3-schema.md:64 specifies a fail-loud precondition: "backlog next / drainable / WIP checks assert the pointer resolves to a real, local epic node and error otherwise". Nothing asserts this. check_epic_wip_cap() (tasks.rs:205) takes a parent_id and never consults active_epic at all, so there is no code path where the pointer's validity is even tested.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE CAP. active_epic is described in ADR-065 as the mechanism behind "one active epic at a time" and is read by backlog focus/next. A pointer that resolves to nothing, or to the wrong project, degrades those to arbitrary results rather than errors — the silent-clean class again (cf. t-2536, t-2546, ADR-069 fail-open).

SCOPE NOTE — establish before fixing: decide whether active_epic should hold an ID (t-2345) or a slug (harness-core). The slug form is what makes cross-project contamination possible (t-1883 exists because of it) and cannot distinguish two projects' identically-named epics. This is a small schema decision but it must be made before writing the assert, or the assert encodes the ambiguity.

AC: resolution is fail-loud — an unresolvable, non-local, or non-epic active_epic errors rather than returning a default or empty result
