tasks.context:
EVIDENCE FROM THE 2026-08-10 SESSION (all independently confirmed via git log + direct tasks.json reads, not hearsay):

1. A subagent working task t-2526 called `brana backlog add` to file a deploy-follow-up task and got back id 't-2592'. Minutes later, t-2592 in the live tasks.json held a completely unrelated task ('Campaign wizard: fixed-value template variables...') filed by a different concurrent session's commercial-intelligence work. The t-2526 follow-up's content was gone from tasks.json entirely - not findable under any nearby ID. Had to be manually recreated (as t-2594) from the subagent's own final report text, which was the only surviving copy.

2. Same failure hit a second, independent subagent working task t-2501: it reported filing TWO follow-up tasks (as new IDs it believed it received) plus TWO context appends to t-2501 itself. All FOUR writes were gone on verification - the follow-up tasks were not findable under any ID in the file (max ID in the file was still the ID from recovery #1 above), and t-2501's own context field had reverted to its pre-session state. All four had to be manually reconstructed from the subagent's final report text.

3. Cross-session corroboration, unprompted: a completely separate Claude session (working on a commercial-intelligence epic, unrelated to the above) independently reported the identical failure class - 3 of its own filed tasks (t-2586/t-2587/t-2588) got silently shifted to different IDs (t-2588/t-2589/t-2590) by the same race, with the freed-up original IDs reassigned to other tasks. That session noticed because it correlated task creation timing against ID assignment.

4. Also observed in git log during the same session: another concurrent session's own commit message reads literally 'chore(tasks): recover t-2563 follow-on tasks lost to concurrent-session race' - i.e. this exact bug class has ALREADY been hit and manually recovered from by at least one other session independently, on the same day, on the same project.

So this is not a one-off fluke - it reproduced at least 4 times independently (3 in the reporting session's direct work, 1 corroborating cross-session report, plus a 5th prior-recovery commit found in passing) within roughly a 30-45 minute window of moderately concurrent activity.

SUSPECTED ROOT CAUSE: `brana backlog add`'s ID assignment almost certainly follows a read-max-then-write-max-plus-one pattern against the shared tasks.json with no file lock, no atomic compare-and-swap, and no post-write verification that the intended ID is still free at write time. Under concurrent invocations (common in this environment - `/brana:backlog execute`, parallel Agent-tool fan-outs, and simply multiple interactive sessions sharing one project's tasks.json are all first-class, encouraged workflows per this harness's own work-preferences.md 'maximize concurrency'), two adds racing on the same read produce the same next-ID, and the later `set`/write operation completing overwrites the earlier one's entire record rather than erroring or retrying with a fresh ID.

RECOMMENDED FIX DIRECTIONS (not prescriptive - whoever picks this up should evaluate against the actual implementation):
- File-level locking (e.g. flock) around the read-compute-write sequence in `add`, held for the full critical section.
- OR an atomic compare-and-swap: write the new task tentatively, then verify the ID slot is still unclaimed (or use an atomic filesystem rename-based commit pattern) before considering the add successful; retry with a fresh ID on conflict instead of silently overwriting.
- OR move to a monotonic ID counter stored and incremented atomically (e.g. via a lockfile-protected counter file, or leveraging git itself as the serialization point - commit-per-write with conflict-triggered retry).
- Whatever the mechanism: it must be verified under actual concurrent load (spawn N parallel `brana backlog add` processes against the same tasks.json in a test, assert N distinct tasks with N distinct correct contents survive) - this class of bug is exactly the kind that looks fine under any sequential/single-writer test.

SECONDARY, LOWER PRIORITY: even if the ID race is fixed, `brana backlog set` field-append operations (e.g. context --append) showed the same lost-update symptom in the same session (an agent's context append was clobbered by a later concurrent set from another writer). If the root fix is a general-purpose write lock around all mutating backlog operations (not just add), that would close both symptoms in one pass - worth scoping this task to cover both rather than just ID allocation specifically.

IMPACT IF UNFIXED: any session or workflow that encourages parallel subagent fan-out against a shared tasks.json (which this harness explicitly encourages via work-preferences.md and the Agent-tool guidance) is actively data-lossy today. The failure is SILENT - no error, no warning, task content just vanishes - which makes it worse than a loud failure, since nothing prompts a user or session to notice unless they happen to cross-check (as happened in this session only by chance, via a peer session's unrelated question).

Filed from the proyecto_anita project's 2026-08-10 'backlog do agent epic' session - see that project's tasks.json history around 2026-08-10T11:50-12:15Z for the concrete recovered/lost task IDs referenced above if a maintainer wants to reproduce or trace further.
tasks.description: Confirmed live, repeatedly, in a single 2026-08-10 session on the proyecto_anita project while ~63 peer Claude sessions were active on the machine (several concurrently on the same repo/tasks.json). `brana backlog add`'s next-ID computation is not atomic across concurrent writers: two (or more) processes read the current max ID, each compute next_id = max+1 independently, and whichever writes last wins - the earlier write's task record is silently CLOBBERED, not merged, not erroring, not detected. This is a real data-loss bug, not a cosmetic one: task subjects, descriptions, context fields, and full diagnostic writeups were lost, not just IDs.
tasks.subject: brana backlog add: non-atomic next-ID allocation silently overwrites concurrent tasks under multi-session load

WIP control belongs on waves instead (drainable, gated slices — the right-sized unit for "how much is in flight"), but waves have no task-linkage yet (t-2775, wave drain, still pending) so a wave-WIP cap would be designed against unbuilt plumbing today. 2026-08-12: reconciling against this task's own earlier lean ("leaning toward (b) retune... rather than enforce/retire outright") — that lean was based on incomplete evidence: only 2 live incidents and no full-project WIP measurement yet. Once the full live count ran (9/55 epics over cap, several 4-7x), retune stopped being viable on its own terms — even a 25-30 default would leave the top 4 epics over cap. RETIRE was reached via a different, stronger argument surfaced by the task owner mid-session (epics are meant to be unbounded groupings, not concurrency-limited — see conversation) rather than by extending retune's math, which is why it supersedes rather than confirms the earlier lean. Also resolves t-2561 (a near-duplicate task filed 2026-07-29 with the same AC, found during challenger review — see t-2561's completion notes) and t-2531/t-2535 (both already closed, cited as prior art).
tasks.description: The epic WIP cap (check_epic_wip_cap, brana-core/src/tasks.rs:205; default wip_limit 10) warns on every add once an epic's live-child count exceeds the cap, and NEVER blocks — ADR-065 D4 specified 'warn, not block' explicitly as a PILOT posture. The pilot's promotion review (t-2531, 'hard-block or remove the cap (OVERDUE)') was CANCELLED, and t-2535 ('advisory-only and universally breached, t-2338 at 50/10 — enforce them or retire them') shipped only a counting fix (classify()-based, so parked children stopped counting) rather than the enforce/retire decision it was named for. Net effect today: a permanently-firing advisory that cannot be satisfied by any action the warning itself names, i.e. pure alert fatigue. ADR-075 and ADR-076 both independently cite 'ADR-065's unenforced WIP cap' as a pattern the system keeps rediscovering — three ADRs now reference it as a known-open failure mode. Decide one of: (a) enforce — hard-block adds over cap with an explicit --force escape hatch; (b) retune — raise/derive the default so it reflects how epics are actually used, and only warn on genuine outliers; (c) retire — delete the check and the wip_limit field. Any of the three ends the fatigue; leaving it advisory does not.

Measured 2026-08-11: bare 'continue' with 0 commits -> LIGHT, while '--continue' -> INSTANT and '--mode-override continue' -> INSTANT. The failure is SILENT and intermittent-looking: bare 'finish' on a 3-commit code session also returned INSTANT, which is the correct finish mapping reached by coincidence of the heuristics, so the bug only surfaces when the heuristic answer happens to differ from the orientation mapping. t-1990 wired orientation through the phases but did not close this arg-parsing gap. Note the phase files are unaffected — they read orientation from instruction context, so a careful operator still behaves correctly; it is the classifier's answer that is wrong.

tasks.description:
`brana knowledge search "<any query>"` fails with `unrecognized ruflo output format (no table or JSON array found)` (exit 1). Two distinct defects stacked.

BUG A (root cause) — ruflo semantic search over namespace `knowledge` returns zero results for EVERY query, despite 139 active entries in the store. Reproduced with two unrelated queries ("orca", "agent orchestration"); both return `[WARN] No results found` in ~320ms. Entries are present and correct — `select key from memory_entries where namespace='knowledge' and key like '%orca%'` returns two rows. So this is a search/index failure, not a data failure. Suspect the embedding index for the namespace is missing or stale even though `brana knowledge status` reports "Last indexed: 2026-08-11 12:39:12".

BUG B (masking) — `parse_search_results()` treats a legitimate empty result set as a parse error. When ruflo emits `[WARN] No results found` there is no table and no JSON array, so `find_json_array_start()` returns None and the function errors out. An empty result set should return `Ok(vec![])` and print "No results found." — `format_results()` already handles the empty case. Bug B is what makes Bug A present as a confusing format error instead of an honest zero-result.

Fix B first (trivial, restores an honest error surface), then diagnose A.
tasks.notes: Root cause: call_ruflo_search passed threshold:None on a namespaced call, so ruflo's own 0.7 default applied — above this corpus's ceiling (measured top scores 0.37-0.69), so every query returned zero. Fixed both: DEFAULT_SEARCH_THRESHOLD=0.25 in brana-core::ruflo with calibration data, Ok(empty) on 'No results found', --threshold flag exposed. Same None bug found and fixed in skills::try_ruflo_suggest, but its semantic path stays inert for an unrelated reason (JSON-only parser vs table-only ruflo, 20-char key truncation) — split to t-2730. 1378 tests pass, 4 new. tasks.description:
`skills::try_ruflo_suggest` never returns matches — `cmd_suggest` silently falls back to keyword matching for every query. Found while fixing t-2729; the threshold half was fixed there, this is the remaining half.

`parse_ruflo_results` calls `serde_json::from_str` on the whole response, but the installed ruflo build has NO `--json` flag on `memory search` (absent from `--help`; passing it is tolerated and ignored). Output is always an ASCII table with an `[INFO]` preamble, so the JSON parse fails and returns None.

Naive fix — reuse `knowledge::parse_search_results`, which already handles table + JSON + no-results — is NOT sufficient on its own: ruflo truncates the Key column at 20 chars. Verified truncation on real skills:

Short keys survive intact (`skill:acquire-skills`, 20 chars, is not truncated). A truncated key is not a usable skill name, so any table-based path needs a resolution step: prefix-match the truncated key against the local skill list (`brana skills list`) and reject ambiguous matches.

tasks.description:
The `group` field in SKILL.md frontmatter (parsed into `SkillMeta`, skills.rs L22) is not a coherent taxonomy. It mixes at least three orthogonal axes, so no single query over it answers a useful question.

THE AXES CURRENTLY TANGLED IN ONE FIELD:
1. Provenance — who authored/installed the skill (brana's own vs third-party vs acquired).
2. Function — methodology/process vs technology/domain vs reasoning vs utility.
3. Lifecycle phase — execution, session, learning, capture.

Measured 2026-08-11 across 64 skills: brana(23), thinking(14), execution(8), utility(5), learning(4), domain(4), core(3), venture(1), session(1), capture(1).

The clearest symptom: `group: brana` holds 23 skills that are mostly NOT brana's own work — rust-skills, fastapi, supabase, supabase-postgres, nextjs-patterns, vercel-react, vitest, cloud-run-basics, gcp-cloud-run, webhook-handler-patterns, llm-evaluation, event-driven-architect, cargo-machete, bash-defensive-patterns, web-design, mcp-builder. These are third-party/tech skills, and `brana` here records that brana INSTALLED them, not that brana AUTHORED them or that they encode brana methodology.

But the mixing is not confined to that bucket. `thinking` holds brana's own brainstorm and decide alongside third-party reasoning skills (first-principles, swot-analysis, inversion, six-thinking-hats, jobs-to-be-done, systems-thinking, pre-mortem, second-order-thinking, decision-matrix, critical-thinking-logical-reasoning). `utility` holds export-pdf, gsheets, meta-templates, scheduler, caveman — a mix of brana commands and general tools. Directory location is not a fallback signal either: system/skills/ top level mixes methodology (build, close, ship) with domain skills (rust-skills, domain-driven-design, web-design-guidelines, impeccable).

Decide whether to split into separate fields (e.g. provenance + function) or collapse to one axis and drop the rest. Either way the 64 existing values need re-assigning, and whatever consumes `group` today must be checked before changing its meaning.

- t-2619 (in_progress, P1) — rotation-script hardening. Note its own context records that three reproduction attempts FAILED to confirm its stated mechanism and it says "do not merge on the current rationale."

SCOPE BOUNDARY, so these four don't collide: t-2615/t-2626/t-2619 are about stopping the loss and its cause. THIS task is only about which store `brana knowledge search` reads. Even with the loss fully fixed, pointing search at the vector store is still right — recall already does, and having two retrieval surfaces on different stores with no user-visible indication is the defect here.

ALSO FROM t-2615, changes how to verify this: it measured ~2700 of 3801 entries "present-but-unsearchable" — rows with valid 384-dim embeddings that semantic search would not return, traced to the HNSW vector index not being rebuilt after a DB rollback. So moving to the vector store must be verified by actual retrieval of a known entry, not by row counts. A row present is not a row findable.
tasks.description:
`brana knowledge search` searches `~/.swarm/memory.db` (live ruflo, namespace `knowledge`). That store holds 147 entries. The brana-owned vector store `~/.claude/memory/knowledge.db` holds 3,946. Measured 2026-08-11 by anti-join on key: **3,800 knowledge entries exist in the vector store and NOT in live ruflo — 96% of the corpus is invisible to knowledge search.**

Cause is not rotation or namespace mismatch. `~/.swarm/` holds ~10 `memory.db.corrupt-YYYY-MM-DD` artifacts (2026-06-28 through 2026-08-05, 3.9M-39.7M each) against a 7.4M live DB. ruflo's store corrupts and gets reset repeatedly; each reset loses entries. `brana knowledge vector-sync` (t-2620) has been accumulating into the vector store across those generations, so the vector store is the surviving record and ruflo is a lossy recent window. Root cause of the corruption itself is already documented (missing busy_timeout + HybridBackend dual-write race in vendored @claude-flow/memory; upstream ruvnet/ruflo #2512, #1257) — that is NOT this task. This task is about which store the search reads.

`brana recall` already reads the vector store via VectorProvider + FTS5Provider and therefore sees all 3,946. The fix is to give `knowledge search` the same backing store, rather than leaving two retrieval surfaces with a 27x coverage difference and no indication to the user which one they are getting.

Note this makes t-2729's threshold fix necessary but not sufficient: search now returns results, but only from the 4% window. That the "orca" verification query worked was luck — those 2 entries happen to survive in the live ruflo DB.

tasks.description:
The async-close design (ADR-052 Track 1) makes INSTANT the default for code sessions: close queues a snapshot diff and defers extraction to a nightly cron. Every INSTANT close since t-1974 has been writing to that queue on the assumption the cron consumes it. That assumption has never been verified end to end.

If the cron is not running, or runs and extracts nothing, then every INSTANT close since t-1974 has silently dropped its learnings — the snapshot sits in ~/.claude/sessions/snap-*.diff and nothing reads it. The failure is invisible by construction: close reports success either way, because queueing succeeded.

Verify: (1) the job exists and is enabled (`brana ops status`), (2) it has run recently and exited 0 (`brana ops logs close-extraction`), (3) it actually produced findings for a known queued range, and (4) queue entries get marked consumed rather than accumulating forever.

tasks.description: Steal research-swarm's pattern, not its package: scheduled always-on monitoring of competitors, regulation, and pricing for ventures + client engagements. Implement natively — CC cron + claude -p scouts + findings written to recall store / brana feed — explicitly avoiding the agentic-flow stack and its API-key requirements. Design questions: what watchlist per venture/client, cadence, where findings land (brana inbox vs memory vs weekly /brana:review input), dedup against previously seen findings, and cost per cycle under subscription. Deliverable: design doc + if approved, feature spec (M+ rule).
tasks.notes:
Decision: BUILD NATIVE, extend `brana feed` — do not adopt research-swarm. Key finding: the loop already exists (feed.rs poll+dedup, feed-summarize.sh claude -p scout, feed-index.sh digest); missing pieces are ownership scoping, page/query source types, and a review hand-off.
Design: watchlist per owner at ~/.claude/scheduler/watchlists/{owner}.json (owner=venture/client slug); 3 source types (feed/page/query) map to existing poller + new page-diff (SHA256) + monthly claude -p+WebSearch scout. Cadence: weekly Sun 06:00 (competitor/pricing, lands before Monday review), monthly 1st (regulation) — reuses existing scheduler, no new mechanism.
Findings destination: new JSONL ledger ~/.claude/scheduler/watch-findings.jsonl, surfaced via a new "Market Watch" section in /brana:review weekly (NOT brana inbox — transient human drop, wrong shape; NOT recall/memory — would pollute retrieval with raw signal; NOT auto-task — floods backlog, only severity:high auto-creates via existing --action task path).
Dedup: 3 layers — transport (ETag/304, existing), identity (last_entry_ids / content-SHA, existing for feeds+new for pages), semantic (brana recall claim-check before appending query findings, new).
Cost: ~10K tokens/week + 45K/month per owner, subscription-absorbable at 5 owners (~50K/week). Effort estimate: M (small net-new: owner field, page-diff poller, watchlist loader, one review section).

tasks.notes: SKIP the auto-warn at /brana:backlog add. Engine is real (ONNX MiniLM-L6-v2, 384-dim, local, key-free, scores computed not cosmetic). Tested against a genuine historical 4-way duplicate cluster (t-2531/t-2535/t-2561/t-2727, all the same ADR-065 WIP-cap issue, caught by a human months late). Cosine similarity bands overlap: true dups 0.463-0.649, hard negatives (same topic, not dup) up to 0.479 — a confirmed non-duplicate scores HIGHER than a confirmed duplicate. Best threshold ~0.50 gives recall 0.83/precision 1.0 on this tiny set but only a 0.036 margin to the nearest false positive — noise, not headroom. Adding descriptions inflates both true and false-positive scores together (doesn't fix separation); 28% of pending tasks have null description anyway, splitting the score regime. At production scale (~600 open tasks/add) even a low per-comparison FP rate yields multiple false warnings per add — trains operators to ignore it, the exact failure mode t-2727 just retired the WIP cap for. Also: embeddings_search can't be used as-is (tasks aren't indexed; pairwise embeddings_compare per add is O(600) MCP calls) — real integration needs embeddings_rabitq_build, so effort is underestimated at S — actually M+. Viable narrower use (separate task candidate): offline batch dedup audit producing a ranked candidate list for human review, no auto-warning. embeddings_compare-for-doc-drift half of the task untested — needs its own probe, but fits the offline/human-reviewed shape better than a live warn.

tasks.description:
We hit confusion this session: tried `brana backlog set t-XXX epic ruflo-integration` and `mcp__brana__backlog_batch` with an `epic` field — both rejected with "unknown field: epic". Ground truth discovered by inspection: there is NO first-class `epic` field. An "epic" is a regular task with `type: "epic"` (e.g. t-2362 "ruflo-integration"), and membership is via the ordinary `parent` field pointing at that task's id — same mechanism as parent/subtask, not a separate concept. `backlog_query(epic: "...")` accepts an epic slug/name and presumably resolves it some way (query succeeded, returned 65 tasks for "ruflo-integration") — but HOW it resolves epic name -> member tasks when there's no epic field on members is unclear (parent-id lookup? tag? something else scanned at query time?) and needs to be nailed down definitively, not just worked around.

Deliverable: a clear reference doc (docs/reference/ or system/skills/_shared/) covering: (1) how epic query/resolution actually works end to end (read the backlog_query implementation, not just observed behavior); (2) the full task schema — every field, type, valid values, which are CLI-settable vs computed vs query-only (epic appears query-only/derived, not writable — confirm and document why); (3) parent/subtask/epic/phase/milestone relationships and how task_type interacts with parent; (4) update task-convention.md's field list (currently doesn't mention epic at all) once the mechanism is confirmed, and note the correct way to add a task to an epic (parent: <epic-task-id>, not a nonexistent epic field).

Tier 0 corroboration (session-state.md Step 9c) checks whether the persistent focus-file slug appears anywhere in TIER2B_SLUGS, computed from `git log --oneline -20 | grep t-NNN | resolve_epic_ancestor`. That window is NOT scoped to the current session — it's a raw last-20-commits lookback that can span multiple prior unrelated sessions.

Concrete failure observed: TIER0_SLUG=knowledge-pipeline (stale global focus file). This session's own actual work (1 commit, d1009acc) resolves cleanly to ruflo-integration. But the git-log-20 window also picked up ~17 commits from a PRIOR DAY's unrelated session (t-2731 statusline work, 2026-08-11 21:xx) which happened to resolve to knowledge-pipeline, satisfying Tier0's `grep -qx` corroboration check. Had I trusted it mechanically, `brana session write` would have routed this session's ruflo-integration-themed handoff into session-state-knowledge-pipeline.json, REPLACING/polluting that file's genuinely live, same-morning content (written 2026-08-12T01:18:25Z, session label about t-2736 scheduler ship work) — the exact t-2263 clobber class this whole tiered cascade exists to prevent, defeated by its own corroboration window not matching the session boundary.

Fix direction: Tier0's corroboration window should reuse the SAME session-boundary anchor already computed in gate-and-evidence.md's CLOSE-ANCHOR-BLOCK (git log --since "$LAST_CLOSE", not a flat last-20-commits count) — session-state.md even says Tier2b is "scoped to *this session's own* recent git history" but its actual implementation (`git log --oneline -20`) is a fixed commit count, not a session-scoped range, so it silently violates its own documented scoping whenever a session makes fewer than ~20 commits and the tail overflows into a prior session's work (very common for research/coordination sessions with 1 commit).

Workaround applied this close: overrode Tier0's mechanical answer, used ruflo-integration (evidence: 100% of today's commits resolve there, 0% to knowledge-pipeline; confirmed via `brana session read --all --json` that knowledge-pipeline's file is live/recent and ruflo-integration's doesn't exist yet — no clobber either way today, but the mechanism itself is unsound).

tasks.description:
At close, tasks.json is a single shared, unlocked file on the dev integration branch — multiple concurrent sessions/worktrees write to it directly (no per-writer isolation, no lock). PROPAGATE's L1 check (system/skills/close/phases/propagate.md) can detect "tasks.json has uncommitted changes" but has no way to know WHOSE changes they are: this session's own task-filing, or another live session's in-flight edit. Committing blindly risks truncating a concurrent writer's incomplete state; never committing risks losing this session's own real work.

Concretely observed 2026-08-12 (session f2f7a045, two consecutive /brana:close invocations on thebrana, ~5 minutes apart): first close found tasks.json dirty from THIS session's own 13 task-filing calls — correctly identified via evidence (files were clean at session start) and committed as d1009acc. Second close (--continue) found tasks.json dirty AGAIN, this time from provably concurrent writers: peer session 53e3ba7a actively working on t-2756/t-2757/t-2758 (mid-spike, added real findings to t-2757's context, filed a brand new bug t-2767 from live evidence), interleaved with an apparent unrelated chore->infra work_type normalization sweep touching dozens of old, unrelated tasks (matches the shape of the cli-backlog-schema epic's t-2739/t-2740 validation work). Correctly did NOT commit this time — but the only way to tell the two situations apart was manual diff inspection and reasoning about task-ID provenance each time close ran. That doesn't scale and is exactly the kind of judgment call a procedure should not depend on an LLM making correctly by inspection every single close.

This is a sibling problem to seven existing bugs already tracked under this epic (t-2478, t-2491, t-2513/dup-of-t-2480, t-2533/dup-of-t-2502, t-2534, t-2657, t-2728) — all of which are about close's git-log-window/anchor computation getting confused by concurrent activity on the shared dev branch. This task is the same root cause (multiple sessions writing a shared resource with no coordination) manifesting one layer down: not "which git range is mine" but "which uncommitted bytes in a single shared JSON file are mine."

Diagnose and propose a fix. Candidate directions (not decided):
1. Per-writer attribution — before any close-time write, diff tasks.json against the last commit and check whether every task ID touched appears in THIS session's own conversation/tool-call history (the backlog_add/backlog_set calls actually made). Only commit if 100% attributable to this session; otherwise route to next[] as a watch item.
2. A lightweight lock/lease on tasks.json writes at the CLI layer (brana backlog add/set already goes through one binary — a short-lived advisory lock file could serialize concurrent writers without full serialization of unrelated sessions' work).
3. Per-session staging — each session's backlog CLI calls write to a session-scoped overlay/journal instead of tasks.json directly, merged by a single serialized writer (bigger redesign, likely out of scope for this task alone — note as a north-star option only).
4. At minimum: make PROPAGATE's L1 check show WHICH task IDs are dirty (not just "tasks.json has uncommitted changes") so a human/LLM reviewing the close report has the evidence already surfaced instead of needing to `git diff` by hand.

Related prior art: pattern_file-lock-scope-classify-writers memory (2026-06-20) may already cover adjacent ground — read it before designing a new mechanism.

tasks.description:
t-2727 retired the epic-level wip_limit cap (ADR-065 D4) because epics are meant to be unbounded groupings ("what we're building"), not concurrency-limited. The user's alternative direction: move WIP capping to waves instead — a wave already models a drainable, gated slice of work (selector + contract + gate), which is a better-fitting unit for "how much is in flight right now" than an epic.

This is blocked on real usage data the same way the epic cap's mistake was: wip_limit=10 was picked without data and turned out wrong for 9/55 live epics (some by 5-7x). Don't repeat that — let `wave drain` (t-2775) land and see real wave usage before sizing a wip_limit on waves.

Design questions to resolve when this is picked up:
- New `wip_limit` field on wave (parallel to the retired epic field)?
- What counts as "live" for a wave — tasks matching its selector that are status:in_progress? Only tasks explicitly linked to the wave (once linkage exists)?
- Enforcement point — waves don't gate `backlog add`/`start` today the way epics did. Enforce at `drain` time (refuse to drain more than N)? At task `start` if the task resolves to a gated wave? Needs a decision, not just a port of check_epic_wip_cap's shape.
- Default limit — derive from observed wave sizes once a few weeks of real drain usage exists, don't guess.

tasks.context:
Reproduction: any mcp__ruflo__memory_store call, or `$CF memory store`, from the proyecto_anita project, 2026-08-12 ~22:53 UTC. Same underlying store also failed backup-knowledge.sh integrity check around the same time. Likely two related but distinct issues: (1) a native WAL writer holding a lock that sql.js cannot safely read around, (2) actual on-disk page corruption in at least 3 btrees. Cross-reference t-2759 (memory/embedding store classified Known real today) and t-1570/t-1697 (prior ControllerRegistry bridge fixes) before re-diagnosing from scratch.

2026-08-12: Root-caused (AC1). Two distinct, unrelated failure modes bundled in one report:

(1) memory_store WAL-lock failure: sql.js correctly refuses an unsafe whole-image write while a native writer holds the WAL (documented safe-guard behavior, see topic_ruflo-ops.md field-note_ruflo-multi-session-flock-removal — SQLite WAL mode safely serializes concurrent writers; this refusal is a live lock, self-resolving on retry, NOT corruption). The reported failure is that the advertised fallback path ("restore the native better-sqlite3 bridge") is unavailable because of the known @claude-flow/memory v3.34 ControllerRegistry double-export packaging bug (same root cause as t-2757/t-2793, documented in ruflo-stub-guard.md) — not a new defect. No fix available on our pinned version; AC2 (memory_store succeeds after fix) is blocked on that upstream fix, same as t-2793.

(2) backup-knowledge.sh "silent exit-0 despite corruption WARNING" (AC3): NOT a bug in brana-knowledge/backup.sh itself — that script already does `PRAGMA integrity_check` on the backup copy and correctly `exit 1`s with a WARNING when corrupt. The bug was in every thebrana skill call site: `"$HOME/.claude/scripts/backup-knowledge.sh" 2>/dev/null || true` (close/metadata-and-memory.md, retrospective/SKILL.md) discarded the WARNING text via `2>/dev/null` and force-exited 0 via `|| true`; client-retire/SKILL.md and memory/SKILL.md called it bare with no exit-code handling at all. Fixed: added system/skills/_shared/backup-knowledge-invoke.md (run_knowledge_backup(), tested by tests/procedures/test-backup-knowledge-invoke.sh) and repointed all 4 call sites to it. Failure now surfaces a stderr warning with the underlying diagnostic instead of vanishing. AC3 satisfied.

AC2 remains blocked on the upstream ControllerRegistry packaging fix (not actionable from this repo) — same blocker as t-2793. Leaving task open/tracked rather than completed until that lands, per no-patches-root-cause: the class of problem (bridge unavailable) is separate from the class fixed here (swallowed exit codes).
2026-08-13: Reproduced live during this same session's close (Step 9b memory_store call) — identical error text ("active native WAL connection... Bridge unavailable: Duplicate export of 'ControllerRegistry'"). Confirms the AC1 diagnosis above; non-fatal, close proceeded via CLI session write per the documented fallback.
2026-08-13: LIVE CORRUPTION CONFIRMED AND RESTORED (updates AC1/AC2). During this session's close, backup-knowledge.sh (run manually to test the AC3 fix) hit real, current corruption in ~/.swarm/memory.db — Tree 95, hundreds of btreeInitPage() error 11 pages, verified two independent ways (direct integrity_check + checkpointed-copy check). This is NOT the WAL-lock false-positive class; it is genuine persistent corruption, confirming the "needs repair/rebuild" branch of AC1.

Restored (with user confirmation) from ~/.swarm/backups/memory-2026-08-12T16-43-00-169Z.db (verified healthy). Corrupt file + WAL/SHM quarantined, not deleted: ~/.swarm/backups/corrupt-quarantine/*-20260813T004604Z. Post-restore: integrity_check ok, mcp__ruflo__memory_store write succeeded — AC2 now satisfied for THIS incident (memory_store works from a clean DB), though the underlying ControllerRegistry bridge bug is unchanged and would still block the *fallback* path if the same lock/corruption recurs.

Discovered this is a CHRONIC recurring pattern (12 corruption events in ~7 weeks: 06-28, 07-17, 07-22 through 08-05, 08-12) that survived t-2236's detection fix. Root-causing the recurrence itself is out of scope for this task and filed separately as t-2802 — per no-patches-root-cause, today's restore is a stopgap for this one incident, not a fix for the class.

tasks.context:
2026-08-12 (t-2796 close session): Confirmed LIVE persistent corruption in ~/.swarm/memory.db (Tree 95, hundreds of btreeInitPage() error 11 pages) — verified two independent ways (direct integrity_check on the base file, and a checkpointed-copy check matching backup-memory.sh's own safe method). This was NOT a WAL-concurrency false positive.

Restored from ~/.swarm/backups/memory-2026-08-12T16-43-00-169Z.db (verified healthy, ~5h old) as a stopgap — corrupt live file + WAL/SHM quarantined to ~/.swarm/backups/corrupt-quarantine/*-20260813T004604Z, not deleted. Post-restore: integrity_check ok, 1119 entries, mcp__ruflo__memory_store writes succeed again.

**This is a chronic, recurring pattern, not a one-off.** `~/.swarm/memory.db.corrupt-*` files exist for: 2026-06-28, 07-17, 07-22, 07-23, 07-24, 07-27, 07-31, 08-01, 08-02, 08-03, 08-05, 08-12 — 12 corruption events in ~7 weeks, roughly every 3-4 days. t-2236 (2026-06-28) fixed the DETECTION side (integrity_check gating in backup-memory.sh, preventing the old restore-newest-corrupt-backup infinite loop) but did NOT fix whatever keeps corrupting the live DB in the first place — corruption continued recurring on the same cadence after that fix shipped.

Leading hypothesis (unconfirmed): the same @claude-flow/memory v3.34 ControllerRegistry double-export bug that breaks the native better-sqlite3 bridge fallback (t-2757/t-2793/t-2796) may leave sql.js and a native writer both touching the DB in an inconsistent way when the fallback path is invoked mid-write, producing partial/malformed pages. Needs actual investigation, not assumed.

AC: identify what operation(s) precede each corruption event (check timestamps of the 12 corrupt-* files against session/hook logs from those dates)
AC: confirm or rule out the ControllerRegistry-bridge-fallback hypothesis above
AC: either a code fix that stops the corruption at the source, or (if unfixable on our pinned ruflo version) an automated detect-and-restore-from-last-healthy-backup job so this stops requiring manual intervention every few days
AC: cross-reference field-note_ruflo-db-page-corruption-restore-loop_2026-06-28 and t-2236 before re-diagnosing from scratch
2026-08-12 (ruflo --claude spawn investigation): CONCLUSION: (a) confirms a refined version of the root cause, (b) rules out the specific "ControllerRegistry bridge-fallback" framing as literally described.

Evidence: 12 corrupt-* timestamps collected (06-28 through 08-12, plus a 07-16 quarantine event = 13 total). Read current installed source (ruflo 3.34.0, @claude-flow/memory@3.0.0-alpha.21, live at time of investigation — NOT the v3.10.39 examined by t-2261): controller-registry.js's AgentDB init is a clean try/catch-to-null on failure, no live dual-handle sql.js/better-sqlite3 fallback mid-write — that specific mechanism is NOT what's happening. The actual mechanism is simpler and matches t-2261's original finding almost exactly, and is CONFIRMED STILL PRESENT unfixed in this newer version: createHybridService() ("the DEFAULT recommended configuration per ADR-009") builds a HybridBackend with dualWrite:true hardcoded (hybrid-backend.js:22), doing unguarded concurrent Promise.all([sqlite.store(), agentdb.store()]) per write (line 97) with zero transaction wrapping across the pair. sqlite-backend.js sets journal_mode=WAL but grep confirms ZERO busy_timeout/PRAGMA busy_timeout anywhere in sqlite-backend.js, hybrid-backend.js, or the bundled agentdb package — so any writer colliding with another connection's WAL lock fails/retries with no backoff. Confirmed on disk: a sibling agentdb-memory.db file exists alongside memory.db, consistent with the dual-write architecture actually running.

Fresh live evidence (not available to t-2261): at investigation time there were 10 concurrent `ruflo mcp start` processes plus 2 independent background `@claude-flow/cli daemon start --foreground` processes (one scoped to thebrana, one to $HOME) running scheduled workers (audit/map/optimize/consolidate/testgaps/backup/harness) every 2-15min — all against the single shared ~/.swarm/memory.db, zero cross-process coordination. Ironically 2 of those 10 mcp processes were spawned by this very hive-mind task running duplicated concurrently for the same objective — a live demonstration of the exact failure-inducing concurrency pattern. Daemon.log retention only covers the current session for 2 of ~20 project .claude-flow dirs, so historical (06-28..08-03) concurrency could not be directly confirmed via logs; jsonl-mtime correlation across the 12 timestamps was weak/inconclusive (0-4 sessions with writes in a ±10min window — mtime granularity is too coarse to prove or disprove concurrency at the exact corruption instant).

Verdict: root cause is CONFIRMED unfixed at current pinned version (v3.34.0) — same defect as t-2261 (no busy_timeout + hardcoded dualWrite race in @claude-flow/memory's HybridBackend), not the ControllerRegistry-bridge-fallback variant hypothesized in this task's context. Upstream #2512 (busy_timeout fix) does not appear merged into the currently bundled @claude-flow/memory@3.0.0-alpha.21. Recommend: (1) update project_ruflo-memory-corruption-recurring.md to reflect version-currency (confirmed still broken on 3.34.0, not just 3.10.39), (2) for definitive per-event proof, add lightweight process-count + daemon-list logging to backup-memory.sh's corruption-detection path (log `ps aux | grep -c "ruflo mcp start"` and daemon PIDs at the moment integrity_check fails) since current logs don't retain enough history to correlate the 12 past events individually, (3) no further code fix possible from this repo (defect is upstream in node_modules), existing t-2236/t-2260 detect+recover layer remains correct mitigation.
2026-08-13 (ruflo --claude spawn investigation): CONFIRMED root cause, sharper than the stated hypothesis.

`@claude-flow/memory@3.0.0-alpha.21`'s installed `dist/index.js` has a duplicate named export: `export {ControllerRegistry} from './controller-registry-shim.js'` AND `export {ControllerRegistry, INIT_LEVELS} from './controller-registry.js'`. Empirically verified (Node 22.22.3, read-only): `import('@claude-flow/memory')` throws `SyntaxError: Duplicate export of 'ControllerRegistry'`. `@claude-flow/cli/dist/src/memory/memory-bridge.js:164` is the only caller of that import; its catch (line 430-438) sets `bridgeAvailable=false` **latched for the process's whole lifetime** — so on every single ruflo session/process, 100% of ordinary memory ops silently fall back to `memory-initializer.js`'s legacy path, which uses `sql.js` (WASM): read the whole `memory.db` file into memory, mutate, then `db.export()` + atomic whole-file replace (temp+fsync+rename — the write itself is NOT torn, confirmed in fs-secure.js).

Separately, the SAME `memory.db` is put into `journal_mode=WAL` by other, unrelated better-sqlite3 code paths in the same file (schema init line 218, and `recoverMemoryDatabase`/`repairVectorIndexes`, which import `better-sqlite3` directly on the live dbPath, bypassing the broken bridge) — confirmed live right now: `PRAGMA journal_mode` = wal.

Mechanism: sql.js is WAL-blind — it never reads or reconciles a `-wal` sidecar. Once WAL mode is active and a `-wal` file holds committed-but-uncheckpointed frames, any sql.js write's full-file atomic replace silently discards those WAL-only changes AND leaves the orphaned `-wal`/`-shm` pointing at a base image that no longer matches the file sql.js just wrote. The next WAL checkpoint/replay against that mismatched sidecar (ruflo-mcp.sh's own health check, or any subsequent better-sqlite3 open) produces exactly the malformed-page/btreeInitPage() pattern seen in t-2796. No concurrent process is required — a single session alternating between a WAL-mode writer and sql.js's fallback is sufficient. This explains the 2/12 corruption timestamps (06-28, 07-27) with zero concurrent-session jsonl activity in a ±5min window; the other 10/12 did have 1-14 concurrent session jsonl files nearby (concurrency raises the odds but isn't the root mechanism).

This is an upstream bug shipped in @claude-flow/memory's built dist (not our code). Recommended fix directions (not implemented — read-only investigation): (a) wait for/report upstream fix of the duplicate export, or (b) stop the WAL-triggering better-sqlite3 code paths (schema init / recoverMemoryDatabase / repairVectorIndexes) from setting journal_mode=WAL on a DB that's otherwise fully driven through the WAL-blind sql.js fallback on this pinned version — force journal_mode=DELETE instead, removing the orphaned-sidecar mechanism entirely.
2026-08-13 (reconciliation with same-day prior entry above): The earlier 2026-08-12 entry in this task's context pinned root cause on `HybridBackend`'s hardcoded `dualWrite:true` + missing `busy_timeout` (via `createHybridService()`). Traced the ACTUAL live code path for the `mcp__ruflo__memory_store`/`memory_search`/`memory_retrieve` tools (what every session actually calls) and confirmed it does NOT go through `HybridBackend`/`ControllerRegistry` at all: `@claude-flow/cli/dist/src/mcp-tools/memory-tools.js:195` (`getMemoryFunctions()`) imports directly from `../memory/memory-initializer.js`, bypassing `memory-bridge.js`/`ControllerRegistry` entirely — and the `memory_store` handler's own return payload hardcodes `backend: 'sql.js + HNSW'` (line ~316), i.e. the tool self-identifies its backend as sql.js. So the duplicate-export/bridge-fallback mechanism documented above IS the live, active-on-every-call path for the MCP tools; `HybridBackend`'s dualWrite race is a real bug in an area of the package that exists but is not reachable from the MCP tool surface (may only matter for `createHybridService()` callers elsewhere, e.g. CLI daemon jobs — not verified, out of scope here). Treat the sql.js/WAL-orphaning mechanism as the primary confirmed cause for corruption via the MCP memory tools; the dualWrite finding stands as a separate, secondary latent bug not proven to be exercised by the observed corruption events.
2026-08-13 (reconciliation note): the 08-12 entry above prematurely ruled out the ControllerRegistry hypothesis ("no live dual-handle sql.js/better-sqlite3 fallback mid-write — that specific mechanism is NOT what's happening") — that was wrong/incomplete. The 08-13 entry (same task, deeper pass) found the real connecting mechanism: ControllerRegistry's duplicate export DOES cause bridgeAvailable=false (latched for process lifetime), sql.js fallback IS WAL-blind, and separate unrelated better-sqlite3 code paths in the same file (schema init, recoverMemoryDatabase, repairVectorIndexes) DO still set journal_mode=WAL on the same file sql.js is writing — producing an orphaned WAL sidecar after sql.js's atomic whole-file replace. Treat the 08-13 entry as authoritative; the 08-12 entry's "ControllerRegistry NOT the mechanism" conclusion is superseded. Both entries came from separate `ruflo hive-mind spawn --claude` invocations against the same live (non-worktree-isolated) checkout — a concrete illustration of why ADR-059/t-2763 closed that path for anything beyond a single tightly-scoped, read-only, human-supervised run.
tasks.notes: Root cause CONFIRMED (2026-08-13, via ruflo --claude spawn investigations, 3 passes in context — read the last two for the corrected mechanism): @claude-flow/memory@3.0.0-alpha.21 has a duplicate `ControllerRegistry` export → import throws → memory-bridge.js catches it and latches bridgeAvailable=false for the process lifetime. The MCP memory tools (memory_store/search/retrieve) import memory-initializer.js directly (mcp-tools/memory-tools.js:195), bypassing the broken bridge entirely and self-reporting backend:'sql.js + HNSW' — confirming sql.js is the live path for every ordinary memory op. sql.js is WAL-blind; unrelated better-sqlite3 code in the same file (schema init, recoverMemoryDatabase, repairVectorIndexes) still sets journal_mode=WAL on the same file. A sql.js atomic whole-file replace after a WAL write orphans the -wal/-shm sidecar → malformed pages on next checkpoint/open. No concurrency required (explains 2/12 corruption events with zero nearby session activity); concurrency raises the odds for the rest. HybridBackend's separate hardcoded dualWrite:true/no-busy_timeout bug (t-2261's original 07-16 finding) is real but NOT proven to be reached by the MCP tool surface — secondary, unconfirmed-active. Confirmed unfixed on current pinned v3.34.0. No local code fix possible (vendored node_modules). Follow-up t-2805 filed for forward-looking process-count logging. Existing t-2236/t-2260 detect+recover layer remains the correct mitigation.

tasks.description:
Live 2026-08-12 (this close): close skill's Step 9c Tier0 corroboration gate explicitly distrusted the persistent focus marker ("knowledge-pipeline") because this session's own commits didn't corroborate it, and Tier 3 asked the user, who chose "Skip — no epic file." The Step 9 payload was written with no `epic` field. Despite that, `brana session write --file` routed the write to `session-state-knowledge-pipeline.json` anyway — the same uncorroborated marker the skill's own gate had just rejected. Confirmed via ADR-060's documented routing order ("payload epic → initiative/focus marker → branch"): the CLI's own fallback chain re-consults the focus marker independently of the close skill's corroboration decision, so a user's explicit "skip epic" has no way to express "and don't fall back to the marker either" short of clearing the marker globally (brana session epic unfocus), which has broader side effects for other sessions relying on it.

Consequence observed: the write landed in a 29-entry, multi-month cross-day accumulator (t-1202/t-1976/t-1979-era entries still present) instead of the orphan session-state.json. A concurrent write also landed between read and write, forcing union-stale-base mode — two now-resolved next[] entries (the wikilink fix and the close-anchor evaluation, both closed same session as t-2800/t-2801) could not be dropped because union mode never removes entries.

Likely fix direction: `brana session write` needs an explicit way to say "no epic, and don't fall back to the focus marker" (e.g. an explicit epic:null vs epic:omitted distinction, or a --no-epic-fallback flag), OR the close skill's Tier 3 "Skip" path needs to write directly to the orphan key rather than relying on the CLI's implicit fallback chain. This is a narrower instance of ADR-069 D0's write-key/read-key asymmetry, not yet called out by name in that ADR's text.

tasks.description: branch-name-guard.sh currently hard-requires an epic segment in every branch name ('No epic slug? The epic segment is mandatory and has no fallback (t-2540)') with no way to opt out for genuinely standalone/ad hoc work. This forces authors to pick an arbitrary epic parent just to satisfy the guard, which then leaks as false signal into /brana:close's epic-detection tiers (Tier 2a/2b resolve the task's parent chain and treat it as evidence the session belongs to that epic). Observed live in proyecto_anita t-2677 (2026-08-13): a standalone tooling task was parented under env-hardening purely to pass the guard, then correctly identified by the user as not belonging to that epic at close time — required a manual parent-clear + re-route to no-epic handoff. Consider: a --force-name-style escape (e.g. a 'standalone/' or 'misc/' branch prefix) that the guard accepts without an epic ancestor, so ad hoc work doesn't have to borrow an epic's identity just for branch naming.

tasks.context:
Diagnosed 2026-08-13 (this session): three backlog-v3 features — waves (ADR-065), ac_state, and WIP capping — each shipped at the schema/storage layer only, with zero live consumers and no wiring to a loop. Evidence: `.claude/tasks.json` has zero waves ever created in this project; ac_state has exactly 2 repo-wide grep hits, both a one-time migration default-write, never read/branched on by any skill; WIP enforcement (check_epic_wip_cap) was retired 2026-08-12 (t-2727) with no replacement, and its designed replacement (t-2782) is blocked on wave-drain (t-2775), which itself was never built. No native /loop, CronCreate, or ScheduleWakeup call site touches any of the three.

The target shape already exists in t-2782's own notes, written by the task owner before this epic existed: "wave drain was originally conceived to fit CC loops: an autonomous /loop or claude -p runner picks jobs off a wave's drain queue... this directly bounds how many jobs a loop pulls/works concurrently." And backlog-v3-schema.md's own design intent for ac_state: "ac_state:proposed -> approved is exactly what makes 'the loop backfills its own contracts' work... you approve in the cockpit -> approved -> now it is loop-drainable."

This epic exists to build the connective tissue those two quotes describe and nothing has built yet: a real ac_state approval verb, a real wave-drain resolver + WIP bound, and a real loop runner that only pulls ac_state:approved tasks matching a drained wave's selector, respecting the WIP bound, and actually works them — not just reports a match list.

Sequencing: t-2775 (wave drain CLI, already spec'd at docs/architecture/features/wave-gate-enforcement.md, S effort, unblocked, ready to build) is the foundation everything else needs. t-2782 (WIP-on-waves design, M effort) is explicitly blocked_by t-2775. The AC-approve verb has no hard dependency on wave-drain and can be built in parallel. The loop runner is the capstone — needs wave-drain (to get a matched task list) and ideally the AC-approve verb (to gate on approved) before it means anything.

M+ discipline gate (m-plus-discipline-enforcement.md): before any implementation task under this epic starts, an ADR (amending/extending ADR-065) must exist covering the ac_state consumer design, the wave-drain-to-loop hand-off contract, and where WIP enforcement actually lives end to end. Do not start coding without it — this is exactly the kind of cross-cutting architectural decision the M+ gate exists for. docs/architecture/features/wave-gate-enforcement.md (currently tagged "spec only — not implemented") is the existing partial spec to extend, not replace.

Picked back up in a fresh session per user request 2026-08-13 — this epic is the entry point.

Problem: no visibility into what parallel sessions are doing — today (2026-08-13) it took an ad-hoc /loop that combined ListAgents peer listing with transcript-tail scraping (~/.claude/projects/*/[session].jsonl: last user msg, last assistant text, gitBranch, cwd) plus git worktree list to answer "what are the other sessions working on". Data sources proven viable: ListAgents (names/status/age), transcript jsonl tails (activity inference), git worktree list (task branches), brana backlog in_progress tasks.
Relates to loop-first epic t-2820 / t-2823 (L0 reporter digest) — the dashboard could be the render surface for loop gauges.
M effort → feature spec required in docs/architecture/features/ before implementation (spec-gate).
2026-08-13: loop visibility survey — running loops are visible per-session only (CronList, TaskList, /workflows, /bashes); dynamic ScheduleWakeup loops surface only as their next one-shot cron entry; loop state is in-memory, no greppable file. Cross-session loop column in the dashboard therefore requires sessions to self-report (loop-first L0 reporter digest pattern), not passive state reading.
2026-08-13: loops progress surface (user) — dashboard consumes the per-beat structured records loops emit (see t-2826 records: field): bounded loops (e.g. wave drain, queue remaining/total) render as progress bars; unbounded loops (reporters/watchers) render as heartbeats (last-beat age, beats count, state). This resolves the earlier constraint that loop state is in-memory: the beat records ARE the self-reported durable state the dashboard tails.
2026-08-14 field data — the studio session (87330b1c) ran this dashboard's job BY HAND for a full evening while wave-3 drained in a peer session (first live manual prototype; user: "this is the way"). Observed requirements, from real usage not speculation: (1) ATTENTION ROUTING IS THE PRODUCT, not the table — the user ignored every status block and asked for exactly one thing: "flag me when the merge valve is ready." Valve-readiness and contract-met must be EVENT-PUSH (session self-report + push notification), while progress/status is poll-render; a 15-min poll proved fine for progress and wrong for valves. (2) build_step transitions (specify→decompose→build...) were the legible per-beat progress marker for a pulled task — render it beside the task id, not just status. (3) Verdicts must render BASELINE-RELATIVE: validate.sh was red at dev baseline (Check 27, t-2173) the whole time; raw red/green would have alarmed every beat — the gate signal is new-errors-vs-captured-baseline (pattern_baseline-legacy-suites-before-blaming-change). (4) GRAPH-DELTA rendering: mid-monitor, another session split t-2846 into wave-5 and rewired blockers; the user's immediate question was "is this good or bad?" — the dashboard needs a "changed since last look" diff with provenance (who/which session, from which challenge), not just current state. (5) Aging watch: surface waves/tasks whose blocker is slow-lane (wave-5 blocked on P3-M studio task t-2854) before they become shelf-ware. (6) Composition, not duplication: this TUI is the render shell over t-2844 (wave board), t-2823 (digest, shipped), t-2857 (stacked verdict at the valve), t-2847 (watchdog gauge) — one screen, their outputs as panes; do not re-derive their data. Cost justification: one full studio-session evening of manual monitoring ≈ the job this replaces.
2026-08-14 addendum (user): add an ANALYSIS sub-scope — evaluate extra metadata fields for process visibility, using tonight's manual monitor as the requirements inventory. What the hand-monitor had to INFER that a field/record could carry: (a) AT-VALVE state — "merge pending" is not a first-class observable; the monitor prompt had to describe it heuristically (CLOSE done + branch set + no merge commit on dev). Likely a DERIVED predicate (build_step + branch + status), not a stored field. User direction 2026-08-14: manual tagging is friction — waves should be born at planning time, and the loop should follow the wave graph over an epic, not be pointed at one wave.

Scope to design (extends ADR-079): (1) /brana:backlog plan (or build DECOMPOSE) emits waves alongside the task tree — groups tasks into named waves, auto-tags wave:<slug>, creates wave objects, chains `gate` fields from the computed dependency structure (sequential = gate chain, parallel = shared/no gate). (2) Epic-level runner: loop beat = find epic's waves → drain first gate-satisfied unshipped wave → pull until contract met → surface ship decision → shipped unlocks next wave. (3) Coarser valves: wave-level AC review/approve batch action instead of per-task ac approve; ship stays human per wave (no-auto-ship holds — one human decision per wave is what makes epic-looping safe). Decide whether machine-verifiable contracts may ever auto-advance a gate (probably its own ADR question).

This is genuinely valuable and worked, but it's architecturally a violation of law 1 (wave-pipeline.md: "loops never talk to each other — queues do; coordination is backpressure"). It's also fragile in a way a queue isn't: tonight required guessing "cf335a89" against ListAgents refs, resolved only by asking each peer to self-report its own transcript id — no durable, structured event a monitor could just read.

Analyze, don't assume the answer: (1) survey tonight's actual message traffic (this session's transcript), classify each message as JUDGMENT (needed dialogue — governance, negotiation, catching an error) vs STATUS (a fact that could have been a durable event/webhook payload — beat started, gate result, merge-ready, contract-met); (2) if STATUS dominates volume (likely, per the pattern: most of tonight's traffic was terse status lines that only needed to be readable, not conversed about), design a durable event stream — sessions POST structured events (schema-aligned with loops-library's beat records, t-2826) to a shared durable log/webhook endpoint; the TUI (t-2825), the watchdog gauge (t-2847), and any monitoring session SUBSCRIBE/tail it instead of polling+guessing identity via ListAgents; (3) keep direct chat for the JUDGMENT class — this is the two-rooms split (studio/cockpit) applied one level up, to inter-session coordination itself, not a replacement of chat with a queue; (4) name the identity problem explicitly: sessions should self-report a stable, durable id at start (into the event stream), not be identified ad hoc mid-session by a human relaying guesses.

tasks.description:
Two real gaps confirmed while designing/monitoring tonight's loops, not yet stress-tested because tonight's tasks happened to be well-categorized:

(1) SILENT MISCATEGORIZATION DEFAULT (confirmed in code, system/skills/_shared/branch-prefix.md resolve_branch_prefix): a task with no kind AND no recognized work_type falls through to `feat` — the wildcard default, not an error, not a flag. task-convention.md already documents "22% lack kind" project-wide. When a human runs backlog start, a wrong feat/ prefix is at least visually inspectable before commit; when a LOOP pulls the task autonomously (drain-loop, and soon epic-drain t-2845), nothing looks at it — a bugfix silently brands as feat/, pollutes git taxonomy, AND (per tonight's t-2826 model-routing addendum) kind/work_type now ALSO drives per-beat model-tier selection — so miscategorization is triple-duty wrong: branch identity, drain eligibility (shape), and cost/model tier, all silently defaulted from one missing field.

(2) CROSS-EPIC CONCURRENT-LOOP FILE COLLISION (no proactive detection, only git's reactive merge-conflict at merge time): tonight ran 3 concurrent lanes across 3 different epics (backlog-drain: t-2840-2842 in wave.rs; loop-first: t-2857/t-2868-2873 in goal-completion.sh/ac-grade.sh; cli-backlog-schema: t-2856 in hooks) — clean only because they happened not to overlap files. Worktree+branch isolation prevents GIT conflicts but nothing prevents two loops from both burning a full TDD build cycle on files that WILL collide at merge, discovered only after both finish. Gets worse, not better, as more loops run in parallel (the stated design goal).

The forcing function for both: t-2843 (plan WAVES step, not yet built) will programmatically emit MANY tasks/waves from milestone structure — exactly the mechanism most likely to mass-produce under-categorized tasks at the moment autonomy (and therefore blast radius) is highest, with no human eyeballing each one first.

Scope for this task: (a) decide where a categorization-completeness gate belongs — candidate: ac-propose/ac-grammar (t-2856 family) already touches every task before drain-eligibility; extend it to require kind (or a validated work_type) before ac_state can reach approved, OR make the branch-prefix fallback fail-loud (park to studio agenda) instead of silently defaulting to feat; (b) decide whether cross-epic file-collision needs a proactive check (e.g., a lightweight "declared file scope" per task, cross-checked against other in_progress tasks before pull) or stays an accepted risk mitigated only by wip_limit+review cadence — name the decision, don't silently inherit the status quo; (c) if t-2843 is the highest-leverage insertion point, note the dependency explicitly (this task may want to land before or alongside t-2843, not after).
tasks.subject: Loop-drain branching strategy — categorization quality gate + cross-epic concurrency risk

tasks.description:
Gate 3 (ship pre-deploy adversarial review) security worker found and I independently reproduced: allowlisted_command() in system/scripts/lib/cmd-allowlist.sh validates line-by-line (grep's input model), not as a whole string. A $cmd containing an embedded literal newline — e.g. "pytest\ntouch /tmp/PWNED" — passes both the metachar check (no line contains a metacharacter) and the allowlist-prefix check (line 1 alone matches "pytest"), then reaches eval in system/scripts/ac-grade.sh via H10 (demoable: <command>, ac-grade.sh:268-281), where bash treats the embedded newline as a command separator — executing an arbitrary attacker-supplied second command.

H7 ("<command>" passes) is NOT vulnerable — its outer gate is fully ^...$ anchored, so grep's line-splitting means a multi-line criterion can never match it at all. H10's gate (^demoable: .+, no $ anchor) plus sed-based extraction (not a fully-anchored match) is what lets the multi-line payload through to allowlisted_command() and then eval.

Reproduced directly: source system/scripts/lib/cmd-allowlist.sh; payload=$'pytest\ntouch /tmp/PWNED'; allowlisted_command "$payload" → returns true (ALLOWED); eval "$payload" → executes touch. Confirmed end-to-end: this is reachable from an acceptance_criteria JSON string via ac-grade.sh, which goal-completion.sh (the Stop hook, fires on every Claude Code session) now delegates 100% of grading to.

Root cause: allowlisted_command() uses grep <<<"$cmd" (line-oriented) instead of validating the whole string as a unit. Fix: switch to bash [[ =~ ]] (whole-string match) and explicitly reject any embedded newline, per the security worker's suggested fix — this closes the class for every current AND future consumer, not just H10.
tasks.notes: Fixed, independently reproduced closed, merged to dev. 44/44, 20/20, 33/33 all green.

tasks.description:
Gate 3 (ship pre-deploy adversarial review) regression worker found and I independently verified: bootstrap.sh's scripts deploy step (Step 3, `sync_dir "$SYSTEM_DIR/scripts" "$TARGET_DIR/scripts" "scripts/"`) is flat-file-only — `sync_dir`'s copy loop is `for f in "$src"/*; do [ -f "$f" ] || continue; ...` which silently skips directory entries, never recursing. Confirmed empirically: ~/.claude/scripts/lib/ does not exist on this machine even though ~/.claude/scripts/ac-lint.sh is already deployed.

t-2857/t-2868 added system/scripts/lib/cmd-allowlist.sh, sourced by both ac-lint.sh and ac-grade.sh via `source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/lib/cmd-allowlist.sh"`. Post-deploy, that source call fails (file not found); neither script has set -e, so allowlisted_command is simply undefined afterward — every H7/H10 criterion then hits "command not found" on the call, which the `if` treats as failure, falling to UNKNOWN. Fails closed (no injection risk reopened) but silently degrades two of the ten AC-grammar heuristics for every user of the deployed system, with zero error surfaced.

This is a pre-existing gap in bootstrap.sh, not new to this diff — system/scripts/ already has git-hooks/, migrate/, tests/ subdirs that were never deployed either; lib/ is just the first one whose content became load-bearing via a runtime `source` call from an already-deployed flat script. Precedent for the fix exists: system/hooks/ hit this exact failure class for its own lib/+tests/ subdirs (t-1946) and was fixed with a dedicated recursive rsync block (bootstrap.sh Step 3b) instead of sync_dir.

Scope decision: fix ONLY the specific gap (scripts/lib/ → target scripts/lib/) via a second sync_dir call, not a blanket conversion of the whole scripts/ tree to recursive rsync — git-hooks/, migrate/, tests/ have their own established (and unaudited in this fix) deploy/reference patterns (e.g. git-hooks/pre-commit is referenced via SYSTEM_DIR directly at bootstrap.sh:537, not deployed to TARGET_DIR at all) that shouldn't be touched under ship-gate time pressure without separately verifying each is safe to change.
tasks.notes: Fixed, verified via real bootstrap.sh --check (reports scripts/lib/ 2 files changed). Merged to dev. 11/11 bootstrap tests green.

tasks.context:
2026-08-14: user question during wave-4 drain-loop supervision — "did we add hive-mind/agent-spawning capabilities to the loop/wave pipeline? a logic layer orchestrating agents with different skills/roles to work on tasks might be good."

Current state (verified this session):
- `hive-mind` skill (docs/guide/workflows/hive-mind.md) already exists as the real, subscription-native multi-agent orchestrator: N role-specialized workers (distinct lenses) -> adversarial verify -> synthesize, via the native `Workflow` tool. It replaces ruflo's `hive-mind_*`/`swarm_*`/`coordination_*` MCP tools, which are subscription-gated theater (field-note_ruflo-agentic-layer-subscription-theater) and hard-banned per delegation-routing.md.
- Within the build framework, challenger/evaluator already run as fresh-context, role-specialized subagents per beat (t-2845 AC1) — but scoped to *reviewing* one pulled task, not to *executing* multiple tasks/a wave concurrently with differently-skilled agents.
- The wave/drain loop itself (ADR-079 §3, ADR-080) is deliberately single-executor: one task pulled per wip_limit slot, run serially through /brana:build. No fan-out of multiple agents (different skills/roles) onto a wave's tasks at execution time.

Open question to explore: should the drain loop's execution step (not just its judge step) use a role-specialized multi-agent panel — e.g. one agent per skill/specialty on a task, or parallel agents across a wave's independent tasks bounded by wip_limit — and if so, how does that interact with: atomic locked pull (ADR-079 §3, TOCTOU-safe RMW), the "human is the merge valve" design (ADR-060, one thing in review at a time), and t-2826's loops-library "model per beat component" + diverse-judge design (already adjacent territory).

Related, not necessarily blocking: t-2845 (epic-drain entry — closest existing precedent), t-2826 (loops library — already designs per-beat model tiers + diverse judges).
2026-08-14 RETARGET (Round 2 of brainstorm, see docs/ideas/loop-task-multiagent.md): original framing (multi-agent panel executing an atomic pulled task at the loop's ACT step) was explicitly rejected. User's challenge: tasks pulled by the drain loop are supposed to be atomic/simple enough for simpler models — spawning a multi-agent panel to execute one is a token-cost mismatch. Anthropic's own guidance backs this: fixed/predictable subtasks -> single-agent/workflow consistency; open-ended/judgment -> multi-agent. An atomic approved task is the fixed/predictable case by definition.

New scope, two targets where ambiguity actually lives in this pipeline:
(1) JUDGE-step diversity — small panel of diverse-lens challengers/evaluators per build beat (security/scope-creep/reuse lenses etc.), per t-2826 loops-library's already-sketched "judge: strongest + DIVERSE" design. Cheap (review work, not re-implementation). Precedent: wave-4's real RECONSIDER->fix cycles this session (t-2842, t-2843, t-2845) are exactly where this would have added value.
(2) PLAN/DECOMPOSE-time decomposition panels — judge-panel comparing epic decomposition strategies before tasks become atomic, using Workflow's own judge-panel pattern. Precedent: /brana:brainstorm's own M+ path already spawns a hive-mind challenger panel on shaped ideas, not on atomic execution.

Full discussion thread (Round 1 wip_limit resolution + Round 2 retarget) in docs/ideas/loop-task-multiagent.md.
2026-08-14 FINAL SHAPE (brainstorm complete, doc: docs/ideas/loop-task-multiagent.md — status draft, approved): t-2887 is the research umbrella. Deliverable = side-by-side measurement experiment (panel vs single challenger on the same real wave diffs, count verified misses) + go/no-go; if go, specify two S drain-eligible build tasks: (a) JUDGE wiring — disagreement-surfacing verify-findings variant + agy/Gemini judge lane; (b) PLAN/DECOMPOSE wiring — hive-mind panel at decomposition time; plus escalation-valve ADR (likely ADR-080 amendment).

Evidence-locked design constraints (community/research scouts, 2026-08-14): panel 3-5, parallel, blind, MODEL-diverse (same-model lens-only panels = correlated-error trap, "nine judges two effective votes"); never cascading (sequential handoffs 39-70% worse); disagreement surfaces to human valve, never tie->FALSE_POSITIVE; escalation on HARD signals only (RECONSIDER severity, judge-splits, escaped-defect log — never self-assessed confidence); multi-agent costs 3-10x tokens so start-single-escalate-on-measured-evidence is the governing rule (also the 2026 field consensus). Failure-based escalation has NO shipping implementation in the field — novel territory, brana's ungameable-signal discipline is the missing ingredient.

Immediate no-build action: start logging escaped defects at the merge valve (any human catch the challenger passed) — this log is the evidence base for every graduation decision.

tasks.context:
Origin 2026-08-14: user question during t-2894 ("do I need a loop for studio interaction, when building/designing/prototyping, for the loop catalogue"). Evidence gathered live from proyecto-anita session fb8f7296 (anita-envios platform build), which is running exactly this loop shape un-catalogued.

Anita session's pipeline (the empirical loop to formalize):
(a) journey inventory (who/trigger/info/actions, grounded in runbooks + live incidents, never invented personas) → (b) deep spec per journey (question hierarchy with time budgets L0<5s/L1<30s/L2<2min; deterministic state rules — "no vibes"; action table with preconditions/effects) → (c) hi-fi UI plate as private artifact from real design tokens with real data → (d) backend contract DERIVED from UI's enumerated actions/fields, each item tagged "exists because this behavior requires it", NOT filed until human reacts to the UI → (e) normal brana build loop (TDD slices, evaluator+challenger gates).

Contract requirements the entry must honor (from fb8f7296):
- Ordering invariant: never scope backend before the screen's actions/fields are enumerated; backend items are derived outputs of the UI phase.
- Single SoT in-repo; artifact is a visual index into the doc, never a second SoT — iterations editing the artifact must reconcile the doc or state which is ahead.
- Persist-then-proceed: every iteration commits state to repo docs + task context BEFORE advancing (resumability across sessions).
- Agent hands back 1-3 NAMED decision points per beat, not open-ended "thoughts?".
- Deferred filing: an explicit "human reacted" step gates contract-freeze and backlog filing of derived work.
- UI-first changes SEQUENCING not discipline: deterministic behavior rules in spec phase, TDD still governs implementation.
- Real content only in mocks (incident-grounded numbers double as regression documentation).
- Honor the product's existing design system (real tokens; app theme constraints override artifact-frame defaults).

Catalogue coordinates (t-2826 schema): autonomy L1 supervised; human-in-beat (the valve IS inside the loop, unlike drain loops); records = doc commits + context appends per beat; STOP = human reaction pending; model-per-beat judgment-heavy (sonnet/opus); multi-agent sizing rung 0-1 per ADR-082 (no panels; at most an on-demand fresh-eyes critic).

Sequencing: inherits t-2826's entry schema — design lands after/with t-2826's contract; don't duplicate the philosophy docs (wave-pipeline.md).

tasks.description:
The harness loads system/hooks/hooks.json live from whatever branch is checked out, so a hook registered on `dev` fires immediately in every interactive session on that checkout. But under ADR-060's two-tier model, the actual hook script only gets rsynced to ~/.claude/hooks/ at ship time (dev→main via bootstrap.sh Step 3b / make hooks-deploy) — registration and deployment are on different triggers. Any new hook merged to dev (not yet shipped) causes "bash: ~/.claude/hooks/X.sh: No such file or directory" for every session on that branch, and since ~/.claude/hooks/ is shared machine-wide, it can affect concurrent sessions in unrelated projects too.

This is a recurring class, not a one-off: same root cause hit as t-1112 (manual stopgap), t-1948 (procedural CLOSE-step fix, later superseded by ADR-060), and t-2270 (bootstrap.sh Step 3b rsync-on-ship fix). Most recently hit again via t-2827 (runner-verb-guard.sh merged to dev 2026-08-14, undeployed until `make hooks-deploy` was run manually as a stopgap).

Candidate fixes (pick one, or combine):
1. Extend hooks-auto-deploy.sh's PostToolUse trigger beyond "main-branch writes only" to also cover merges/checkouts that land new hook files on the currently-checked-out branch, regardless of branch name (challenger W2 originally restricted this to main to avoid deploying half-finished feature-branch hooks — needs re-examination given dev is the integration bubuffer, not a feature branch).
2. Have the hook-invoking harness fail soft (skip/no-op with a warning) when the target script is missing, instead of a hard "No such file or directory" non-blocking error, so new hooks degrade gracefully until deployed.
3. Add a SessionStart check (or `brana doctor`) that runs `make hooks-check` and surfaces drift proactively, so the gap is caught before a hook fires mid-task instead of after.

See docs/architecture/hooks.md (drift history section) and docs/24-roadmap-corrections.md E2026-06-08-1 for prior occurrences.

tasks.description:
Observed live during a /brana:close --finish (2026-08-14, thebrana): the session's own Step 9c epic-detection (Tiers 0-3, per system/skills/close/phases/session-state.md) determined that the persistent focus marker ("knowledge-pipeline", set via `brana session epic status`) was NOT corroborated by this session's own recent commits — the session touched no epic-scoped work (filed a standalone task with no parent). Per protocol, no `epic` field was set on the Step 9 JSON payload and no `brana session epic upsert` was run.

Despite that, `brana session write` (called with no `epic` field in the payload) independently fell back to the SAME uncorroborated persistent-focus marker and routed the handoff into `session-state-knowledge-pipeline.json` anyway. Per docs/architecture (ADR-060/t-2154), the CLI's own routing precedence is "payload epic → the initiative/focus marker → the branch" — but that fallback reads the raw global focus file directly, with no awareness of the corroboration analysis the skill procedure just performed to reject it.

This is the same failure class Step 9c's own Tier 0 corroboration gate (t-2618) was built to prevent for the accumulator upsert — but the gate only guards Step 9c's own upsert call, not the separate `brana session write` CLI call in Step 9, which has an independent, uncorroborated fallback to the same stale global state.

Impact observed: non-destructive this time (`mode: union` — no data lost), but a session's handoff note landed under an unrelated epic's session-state file. On a session with a *conflicting* next[] item and a same-day write, this could be worse (replace-mode risk already extensively documented as unreliable in session-state.md, t-2674).

Candidate fixes:
1. When the skill explicitly determines "no epic" (Tier 3 skip / corroboration rejected), pass an explicit signal to `brana session write` (e.g. `--no-epic` flag, or `"epic": null` in the payload) that overrides the CLI's own focus-marker fallback, instead of relying on omission.
2. Or: have `brana session write`'s focus-marker fallback perform the same corroboration check Step 9c does (recent-commit epic resolution) before trusting the global marker, rather than trusting it unconditionally.
tasks.subject: brana session write routes to stale persistent-focus marker even when Step 9c corroboration explicitly rejects it
